meta.blurb: On a hot Sunday, Anya asks her uncle Ravi what the universe really is. He has a chalkboard, a teapot and five hours to answer. By six o'clock, the board is full of her own questions.
meta.bible: Anya: a curious teenager who asks big questions. Ravi: her uncle, a retired physics teacher with a chalkboard and a big teapot. Setting: Ravi's garden, one hot Sunday afternoon from one o'clock to six o'clock, with one idea for each stretch of the afternoon. Real facts used: the universe began almost fourteen billion years ago in the Big Bang; the Cosmic microwave background was found in 1965; about five percent of the universe is ordinary matter, about a quarter is Dark matter and about seven tenths is Dark energy; Dark energy was found in 1998 from exploding stars; gravitational waves were first detected in 2015 and a pair of colliding Neutron stars was seen in 2017; the first picture of a black hole was shown in 2019; the Hubble telescope was launched in 1990 and the Webb telescope in 2021; Einstein's theory of gravity, called General relativity, dates from 1915. Key terms: Atom, Nucleus, Gravity, Electromagnetism, Spectrum, Redshift, Doppler, Helium, Hydrogen, Antimatter, Galaxy, Supernova, Exoplanet, Telescope, Infrared, Photon, Proton, Neutron, Quark, Carbon, Oxygen, Iron, Gold, Milky Way, Andromeda, Sun, Earth. Timeline: the whole history of the universe is squeezed into five hours, so the Earth forms at about twenty past four and people appear in the last half second. Voice: relaxed, funny and clear; numbers are real or marked "about"; where scientists do not know, the book says so. FULL-LENGTH BOOK (200 beats, 20 chapters of ten beats, the afternoon runs from one o'clock to six o'clock, about fifteen minutes of afternoon per chapter): Extra characters and props: Kepler is Ravi's old grey cat, who sits on the gatepost; the garden has an old Plum tree, a Chalkboard on an Easel, a big brown Teapot, ginger biscuits, a camping stove, a Prism, a garden hose, an old Mattress, marbles, a Balloon, a bowl of bread dough with Raisins, a bicycle pump, an old television and a Periodic table poster pinned to the shed door; Anya rides a bicycle and writes in a Notebook. Chalk clock: Ravi squeezes cosmic history onto a chalk clock where one o'clock is the Big Bang and six o'clock is today, about 46 million years a minute: first stars a few minutes after one, the Sun and Earth at about twenty past four, life at about twenty-three minutes to five, oxygen at about ten past five, animals at about a quarter to six, dinosaurs from about five minutes to six until about a minute and a half before six, our species about half a second before six. The chalk clock is not the real time in the garden. More real facts used: the Sun is about a million times the volume of the Earth, which is about 12,700 kilometres wide; light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second and takes about eight minutes from the Sun; the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years wide and the Sun is about 26,000 light-years from its centre and circles it once in about 230 million years; Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away; Newton published his law of gravity in 1687; Einstein's General relativity dates from 1915 and starlight bending was seen in the eclipse of 1919; Fraunhofer mapped dark lines in 1814, Kirchhoff and Bunsen explained them in 1859, Helium was found in the Sun in 1868; Cecilia Payne showed in 1925 that stars are mostly Hydrogen and Helium; Christian Doppler explained the Doppler effect in 1842; Friedrich Bessel measured the first star distance in 1838; Henrietta Leavitt found the pulsing-star rule around 1912; Edwin Hubble found that Andromeda is a galaxy in 1923 and published Hubble's law in 1929; Vesto Slipher measured galaxy redshifts from 1912; Georges Lemaitre proposed the primeval atom in 1931; Fred Hoyle named the Big Bang in 1949; Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman predicted the afterglow in 1948; Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the hiss in 1964 and won the Nobel Prize in 1978; the afterglow was set free about 380,000 years after the start and is now less than three degrees above absolute zero; COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped it, with ripples of about one part in 100,000; Alan Guth proposed Inflation in 1980 (not proven); Carl Anderson found the positron in 1932; helium was made in the first few minutes, three quarters Hydrogen to one quarter Helium by mass; the Sun turns about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second; Jocelyn Bell found the first pulsar in 1967; a neutron star is about twenty kilometres wide; supernova of 1054 (Crab Nebula), supernova of 1987 in the Large Magellanic Cloud with neutrinos; Orion Nebula about 1,300 light-years away; Galileo saw the stars of the Milky Way in 1610; the Local Group is about ten million light-years wide; Virgo Cluster about 55 million light-years away; Laniakea was mapped in 2014; Fritz Zwicky noticed missing mass in the Coma cluster in 1933; Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured flat galaxy rotation in the 1970s; the Bullet Cluster was studied in 2006; MOND was proposed by Mordehai Milgrom in 1983; the LUX-ZEPLIN xenon detector is in South Dakota and the Large Hadron Collider is at CERN near Geneva; the two supernova teams of Saul Perlmutter and of Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess found acceleration in 1998 and won the Nobel Prize in 2011; the DESI survey hints that dark energy may change (not settled); John Michell imagined dark stars in 1783 and Karl Schwarzschild solved the black hole equations in 1915 and 1916; Cygnus X-1 was the first strong black hole candidate in 1971; the star S2 circles Sagittarius A star every sixteen years (Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez, Nobel Prize 2020); the Event Horizon Telescope showed M87 in 2019 and Sagittarius A star in 2022; Hulse and Taylor found the binary pulsar in 1974; LIGO (Louisiana and Washington State, arms four kilometres long) detected two merging black holes on 14 September 2015, announced in February 2016, Nobel Prize in 2017 for Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne; two neutron stars merged about 130 million light-years away on 17 August 2017 and the kilonova showed gold; LISA is a planned space detector; Hafele and Keating flew clocks round the world in 1971; the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across; Hubble was launched in 1990 and repaired in 1993, the Hubble Deep Field was taken in 1995; the James Webb telescope was launched on Christmas Day 2021 and sits about one and a half million kilometres from Earth; the Extremely Large Telescope is being built in Chile and the Square Kilometre Array in Australia and South Africa; Gaia has mapped nearly two billion stars; Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b in 1995 (Nobel Prize 2019); Kepler was launched in 2009; TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-sized planets about 40 light-years away; Europa and Enceladus may hide oceans and Europa Clipper is on its way; the Murchison meteorite fell in Australia in 1969 with more than seventy amino acids; Frank Drake began listening for signals in 1960 and the Wow signal came in 1977; Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and photographed the Earth as a pale dot in 1990; the Parker Solar Probe reaches about 190 kilometres a second; Breakthrough Starshot is only a proposal; Miguel Alcubierre described a warp bubble in 1994; the universe looks flat on large scales; Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that black holes should slowly evaporate; Theia is the name given to the planet that hit the young Earth. Small props: a Paperclip lifted by a fridge magnet, a Raisin in the dough, a Teapot, a Chalkboard. Voice: unchanged. Where scientists are unsure the book says so (dark energy, inflation, the multiverse, the Andromeda collision, the Hubble tension).

beats.scene: Anya leans her bike on Ravi's gate while an old cat watches
beats.summary: At one o'clock on a hot Sunday, Anya cycles to her uncle Ravi's house with a notebook full of questions.

beats.scene: Ravi carries a chalkboard and a huge teapot across the lawn
beats.summary: Ravi sets up a chalkboard, a big teapot and a plate of ginger biscuits under the plum tree.

beats.scene: Anya sits on the grass and points up at the sky
beats.summary: Anya asks what the universe really is, and why nobody can explain it in plain words.

beats.scene: Ravi writes the word universe on the board and underlines it twice
beats.summary: Ravi says the universe is everything that exists: all space, all time, all matter and all energy.

beats.scene: Ravi taps a rule written at the bottom of the chalkboard
beats.summary: Ravi sets one rule: ask anything, and when nobody knows the answer, say so honestly.

beats.scene: Ravi taps a clock face drawn at the top of the chalkboard
beats.summary: Ravi says they have five hours, from one o'clock until six, with one big idea for each stretch.

beats.scene: Anya stands beside a chalk line marking her height on the board
beats.summary: Ravi starts a ladder of sizes with Anya, who is about a metre and a half tall, and climbs to a tree, a mountain and the Earth.

beats.scene: A huge chalk circle for the Sun beside a tiny dot for the Earth
beats.summary: The Sun is about 109 Earths wide, and about a million Earths would fit inside it.

beats.scene: A spiral of chalk dots with a tiny arrow marking the Sun
beats.summary: The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, a galaxy so wide that light takes about 100,000 years to cross it.

beats.scene: Ravi carries his chalk line along the garden fence beyond the board
beats.summary: The universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, so the board is too small, and Ravi carries the line along the fence.

beats.scene: Ravi holds a magnifying glass over a plum-tree leaf
beats.summary: Ravi turns the ladder upside down: a leaf is built of tiny cells, much smaller than a grain of sand.

beats.scene: A single drop of water on Anya's fingertip catches the sun
beats.summary: A single drop of water holds more than a billion billion molecules, each made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

beats.scene: A pea sits in the middle of a huge empty football stadium
beats.summary: Everything is built of atoms, and an atom is nearly empty: its nucleus is to the atom as a pea is to a stadium.

beats.scene: A fuzzy cloud drawn around a dot, like a small blurred swarm
beats.summary: Electrons are not tiny planets in orbit; they form a fuzzy cloud, and we can only say where one is likely to be.

beats.scene: A small chalk table lists hydrogen, carbon and gold with their numbers
beats.summary: The number of protons in the nucleus decides the element: one for hydrogen, six for carbon and seventy-nine for gold.

beats.scene: A proton drawn as a circle holding three small dots
beats.summary: Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks, and nobody has found anything smaller inside a quark.

beats.scene: Anya presses her palm against the wooden garden table
beats.summary: A table feels solid because electric forces between electrons push back, so Anya's hand never truly touches it.

beats.scene: Four chalk arrows are labelled with the names of the four forces
beats.summary: Ravi lists the four forces of nature: gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak forces inside atoms.

beats.scene: A small fridge magnet lifts a paperclip off the garden table
beats.summary: A small magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the whole Earth, which shows how weak gravity is.

beats.scene: A tiny chalk arrow beside a huge arrow wrapped around a galaxy
beats.summary: Gravity wins over large distances because it only pulls, while electric charges cancel each other out.

beats.scene: A ripe plum drops from the tree onto the grass beside Anya
beats.summary: Newton wondered whether the pull that brings a falling fruit down also holds the Moon in its path.

beats.scene: A chalk cannon on a tall mountain fires balls that land farther each time
beats.summary: A cannonball fired harder lands farther away; fired fast enough, it keeps falling around the Earth, which is an orbit.

beats.scene: A chalk graph shows a pull that shrinks quickly as distance grows
beats.summary: Newton's law of 1687 says that the pull grows with mass and weakens with distance: twice as far means four times weaker.

beats.scene: An old quill lies beside a page covered in Newton's sums
beats.summary: Newton could say how gravity behaves, but he admitted that he did not know what it is or why it works.

beats.scene: Ravi lies on a mattress on the lawn while marbles roll towards him
beats.summary: In 1915 Einstein said that mass bends space, and bent space makes things fall: gravity is the shape of space and time.

beats.scene: Marbles circle a heavy ball resting on a stretched sheet
beats.summary: Mass tells space how to curve, and curved space tells mass how to move; the planets follow the straightest path they can.

beats.scene: Mercury's oval orbit slowly turns round the Sun, drawn in chalk
beats.summary: Newton's law could not quite explain how Mercury's orbit slowly turns, but Einstein's new theory got the number right.

beats.scene: Astronomers record stars beside a darkened Sun during an eclipse
beats.summary: In 1919, during a total solar eclipse, astronomers saw that starlight bends around the Sun, just as Einstein had predicted.

beats.scene: A satellite circles the Earth with a tiny clock on its side
beats.summary: GPS satellites need Einstein's theory: without it their clocks would drift and positions would be wrong by about ten kilometres a day.

beats.scene: Anya and Ravi write the word spacetime on the board with an arrow
beats.summary: Time bends too: space and time are woven into one fabric called spacetime, and Anya explains the idea back in her own words.

beats.scene: A torch beam races from the lamp to the far garden fence
beats.summary: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second, fast enough to go seven and a half times round the Earth in one second.

beats.scene: A beam of sunlight leaves the Sun and crosses a long gap of space
beats.summary: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, so we always see the Sun as it was a little while ago.

beats.scene: Chalk dots show the nearest stars with their distances in years
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about nine and a half trillion kilometres; the nearest star beyond the Sun is over four light-years away.

beats.scene: The pale oval of the Andromeda galaxy shines in a dark night sky
beats.summary: The Andromeda galaxy is about two and a half million light-years away, so we see it as it was before our species existed.

beats.scene: A chalk rocket needs a bigger and bigger fuel tank as it speeds up
beats.summary: Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light, because the faster something moves, the more energy it takes to speed it up.

beats.scene: Ripples spread across a bowl of water on the garden table
beats.summary: Light behaves like a wave, like ripples on a pond, and also like a stream of tiny packets called photons.

beats.scene: Sunlight through a glass prism spreads a rainbow across the grass
beats.summary: A prism splits sunlight into a rainbow, as Newton showed in 1666: white light is a mixture of all the colours.

beats.scene: Ravi shakes a long garden hose to make short and long waves
beats.summary: The length of a wave decides the colour: red has the longest wavelength we can see and violet the shortest.

beats.scene: A long chalk line with a tiny rainbow slice in the middle
beats.summary: Our eyes see only a thin slice of all light; radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are invisible.

beats.scene: Anya's phone screen shows a purple glow from a remote control
beats.summary: Telescopes can see every kind of light, and even a phone camera can see the infrared glow of a television remote.

beats.scene: A rainbow strip crossed by dark lines like a barcode
beats.summary: At two o'clock Ravi shows that the Sun's rainbow has hundreds of dark lines, first mapped by Fraunhofer in 1814 and linked to the chemical elements in 1859.

beats.scene: Salt sprinkled into a camping-stove flame turns it bright yellow
beats.summary: Every element glows with its own colours, so the lines in a star's rainbow are fingerprints that show what the star is made of.

beats.scene: A bright yellow line in the Sun's rainbow that matches no known element
beats.summary: In 1868 astronomers found a line in sunlight that matched no known element; they named it helium, after the Greek word for the Sun, and it was found on Earth in 1895.

beats.scene: A young woman at a desk in Harvard writes about the stars
beats.summary: In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed from star spectra that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, though experts at first did not believe her.

beats.scene: An ambulance with a siren drives past, with wavy lines in front and behind
beats.summary: A siren sounds higher as it comes and lower as it goes: the Doppler effect, explained by Christian Doppler in 1842.

beats.scene: A wavy line is stretched when moving away and squeezed when coming closer
beats.summary: Light does the same: a source moving away looks redder, and one moving closer looks bluer, so the shift in the dark lines tells its speed.

beats.scene: Anya holds her thumb at arm's length and winks with each eye in turn
beats.summary: Nearby stars shift against the background as the Earth circles the Sun, which gives their distance, but this works only for stars that are fairly close.

beats.scene: A tray of old glass plates with some star dots circled in ink
beats.summary: Around 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that brighter pulsing stars pulse more slowly, so timing a star tells its true brightness, and comparing that with how dim it looks gives its distance.

beats.scene: A big telescope dome on a mountain under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: In 1923 Edwin Hubble found one of Leavitt's pulsing stars in Andromeda; its distance showed that Andromeda is another galaxy far outside the Milky Way.

beats.scene: A graph of dots rising in a straight line from near to far galaxies
beats.summary: In 1929 Hubble showed that nearly all galaxies are moving away, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves: Hubble's law.

beats.scene: A bowl of dough with raisins swells under a tea towel
beats.summary: Anya fears that Hubble's law puts the Milky Way at the centre, but rising dough with raisins shows that every raisin sees the others move away.

beats.scene: Dots drawn on a balloon spread apart as Anya blows it up
beats.summary: Galaxies are not flying through space; space itself is stretching, like the surface of a balloon, so there is no centre and no edge.

beats.scene: Ravi draws the loaf shrinking back into a tiny glowing dot
beats.summary: Run the expansion backwards and the universe was once very hot and dense, nearly fourteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: Chalk dots spread outwards everywhere on the board, with no centre mark
beats.summary: The Big Bang was not an explosion in one place but space stretching everywhere at once; Lemaître proposed it, and Fred Hoyle named it on the radio in 1949.

beats.scene: Two chalk columns on the board: Steady State and Big Bang
beats.summary: Hoyle's rival Steady State theory said the universe never changed, but in 1948 Alpher and Herman calculated that a hot beginning should have left a faint glow across the sky.

beats.scene: A huge white horn-shaped radio antenna on a hill in New Jersey
beats.summary: In 1964 the radio engineers Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found a faint hiss, coming from every direction, in a big horn antenna in New Jersey.

beats.scene: Two pigeons sit inside a big radio horn while a man scrubs it clean
beats.summary: They even cleaned out pigeon droppings, but the hiss stayed, until a team at Princeton realised that it was the afterglow of the Big Bang.

beats.scene: A wall of orange fog thins into clear space
beats.summary: The hiss is the first light of the universe, set free about 380,000 years after the start and stretched by expansion into microwaves less than three degrees above absolute zero.

beats.scene: An old television in the shed shows grey snow on its screen
beats.summary: A small part of the static on an old analogue television is this ancient light.

beats.scene: A map of the whole sky in faint blue and orange patches
beats.summary: Satellites named COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped the glow and found tiny differences, about one part in 100,000, which were the seeds of the first galaxies.

beats.scene: Ravi draws a long timeline with a question mark at its left end
beats.summary: We can follow the story back to a tiny fraction of a second after the start, but at the very first instant our theories break down.

beats.scene: Ravi's chalk dot swells quickly into a huge circle
beats.summary: In 1980 Alan Guth suggested that in the first tiny fraction of a second the universe swelled enormously fast; this idea, inflation, would explain its smoothness but is not proven.

beats.scene: A tiny glowing dot labelled hotter than any star, in the first second
beats.summary: In the first second the universe was a hot soup of energy and particles, and Einstein's famous equation shows how energy can turn into matter.

beats.scene: Loose quarks gather into groups of three as the board cools
beats.summary: Within about a millionth of a second, as the universe cooled, quarks joined in threes to make the first protons and neutrons.

beats.scene: A particle and its mirror twin meet in a bright flash on the board
beats.summary: Every particle has an antiparticle twin, and when matter meets antimatter, both vanish in a flash of energy; the first antiparticle was found in 1932.

beats.scene: A scale with a tiny extra weight on the matter side
beats.summary: A tiny excess of matter survived, about one extra particle for every billion pairs, and everything we see is made from that leftover; nobody knows why.

beats.scene: Two small balls, one yellow and one blue, are made in a hot cloud
beats.summary: Within the first few minutes, protons and neutrons fused into helium nuclei, in a brief window of cosmic cooking that lasted about twenty minutes.

beats.scene: A circle divided into three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium
beats.summary: The result was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass; the cooking stopped because the universe became too cool and thin, so heavier atoms had to wait for stars.

beats.scene: A glowing orange fog clears as electrons settle onto nuclei
beats.summary: For 380,000 years the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles that trapped light; when it cooled enough for atoms to form, the fog cleared and light flew free.

beats.scene: A dim cloud of gas with slightly denser patches pulling in more gas
beats.summary: After the fog cleared, the universe was dark for a long time while gravity slowly pulled gas into the denser patches that would become the first stars and galaxies.

beats.scene: The first stars switch on like distant lamps in a dark sky
beats.summary: The first stars switched on perhaps a hundred or two hundred million years after the Big Bang, and Webb has seen galaxies from less than 300 million years after the start, some brighter than expected.

beats.scene: Anya pumps up her bicycle tyre and feels the pump grow warm
beats.summary: A collapsing cloud of gas heats up like a bicycle pump; at about ten million degrees in its centre, hydrogen starts to fuse and a star is born.

beats.scene: Four hydrogen dots join into one helium dot with a small flash
beats.summary: In the Sun's core four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus and a little mass turns into energy: about four million tonnes of the Sun every second.

beats.scene: A balloon squeezed in two hands, with the air pushing back
beats.summary: A star is a balance: gravity squeezes it inwards while the heat of fusion pushes outwards, and the balance can last for billions of years.

beats.scene: A spark of light bounces through a dense maze inside the Sun
beats.summary: Light made in the Sun's core takes many thousands of years to struggle out through the dense gas, but only about eight minutes to reach the Earth.

beats.scene: A huge blue star and a small red star shine side by side
beats.summary: Big stars burn fast and die young after a few million years, while small red dwarf stars burn so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years.

beats.scene: A star swells into a red giant above a chalk drawing of a kitchen
beats.summary: When a star's core runs out of hydrogen it swells into a red giant, and helium begins to fuse into carbon and oxygen.

beats.scene: Ravi cuts an onion in half beside a chalk drawing of a layered star
beats.summary: A heavy star builds up layers like an onion, fusing carbon, then oxygen, then silicon, until its core is made of iron.

beats.scene: A star's core collapses and its outer layers blast away in bright gas
beats.summary: Fusing iron takes in energy instead of giving it out, so a heavy star's core collapses in a second and the star explodes as a supernova, for weeks as bright as a whole galaxy.

beats.scene: An old scroll shows a bright new star beside a crab-shaped cloud
beats.summary: Chinese astronomers recorded a supernova in 1054, whose remains are the Crab Nebula; a supernova in 1987 sent ghostly particles called neutrinos that were detected hours before its light.

beats.scene: A glowing ring of gas surrounds a tiny white star, like a smoke ring
beats.summary: At three o'clock Ravi turns to smaller stars: a star like the Sun does not explode but sheds its outer layers, leaving a hot white dwarf about as big as the Earth.

beats.scene: A white dwarf pulls a stream of gas from a nearby red star
beats.summary: A white dwarf in a close pair can pull gas from its companion until it explodes as a Type Ia supernova, which has nearly the same brightness every time and so can measure distance.

beats.scene: A tiny dense ball drawn on a city map, heavier than the Sun
beats.summary: The collapsed core of a heavy star can survive as a neutron star, about twenty kilometres wide but heavier than the Sun, so that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.

beats.scene: A cartoon lighthouse beam sweeps round a tiny spinning star
beats.summary: In 1967 a student, Jocelyn Bell, found a radio signal that pulsed once every second and a third; it came from a spinning neutron star, now called a pulsar.

beats.scene: A glowing gas cloud gathers into new stars, with the young Sun among them
beats.summary: Gas thrown out by dying stars mixes with clouds and forms new stars; the Sun, born about four and a half billion years ago, is a later generation, enriched with elements from earlier stars.

beats.scene: A rocky planet forms from grains of dust clumping around a young star
beats.summary: Without heavy elements there could be no rocky planets, no oceans and no air to breathe; the first stars had only hydrogen and helium to work with.

beats.scene: A periodic table poster coloured by where each element was made
beats.summary: Ravi pins up a periodic table coloured by origin: hydrogen from the Big Bang, carbon and oxygen from stars, iron from exploding stars, and a few of the heaviest elements still uncertain.

beats.scene: Anya looks at her own hand beside a chalk periodic table
beats.summary: Most of the atoms in Anya's body are hydrogen from the Big Bang, while the carbon, calcium and iron in her were made inside stars.

beats.scene: Anya's notebook with the number fourteen billion circled beside a hydrogen atom
beats.summary: The hydrogen in Anya is almost as old as the universe itself; atoms are only borrowed, having been part of other things before and passing to others later.

beats.scene: The fuzzy glow of the Orion Nebula beneath three stars in a row
beats.summary: New stars are being born now, for example in the Orion Nebula, a cloud about 1,300 light-years away that can be seen with the naked eye on a winter night.

beats.scene: A spiral galaxy, a round oval galaxy and a small untidy galaxy
beats.summary: Gravity gathered stars into galaxies of different shapes: spirals, ovals and untidy irregulars.

beats.scene: A barred spiral galaxy with the Sun marked far from the centre
beats.summary: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral with a bar across its middle; the Sun is about 26,000 light-years from the centre, in a quiet arm.

beats.scene: A pale band of stars arches over a dark garden at night
beats.summary: On a dark night the Milky Way looks like a pale band across the sky; in 1610 Galileo saw with his telescope that it is made of countless stars.

beats.scene: A chalk spiral with a long curved arrow showing the Sun's path
beats.summary: The Sun circles the centre of the galaxy once every 230 million years, so the last time it was here, the first dinosaurs were only just appearing.

beats.scene: Two fuzzy patches in the southern sky beside the Milky Way
beats.summary: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies that circle the Milky Way and can be seen with the naked eye from the southern half of the world.

beats.scene: Chalk blobs for the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum with small companions
beats.summary: The Milky Way, Andromeda, the smaller Triangulum and dozens of dwarf galaxies form the Local Group, about ten million light-years wide, held together by gravity.

beats.scene: A tight bundle of chalk dots labelled Virgo, far off on the board
beats.summary: Groups gather into clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, such as the Virgo Cluster, about 55 million light-years away.

beats.scene: A foam of bright threads surrounds dark empty bubbles
beats.summary: Clusters are linked by long filaments around giant empty voids, forming the cosmic web; in 2014 astronomers mapped our home region, Laniakea.

beats.scene: A tally of chalk marks that covers the whole garden fence
beats.summary: The observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, perhaps more, many with hundreds of billions of stars, yet most of space is almost empty.

beats.scene: Two galaxies pass through each other while tiny dots drift between them
beats.summary: Galaxies sometimes collide, but their stars almost never hit each other, because the gaps between stars are enormous.

beats.scene: Arrows on the board show galaxies in a cluster moving far too fast
beats.summary: In 1933 Fritz Zwicky found that the galaxies of the Coma cluster moved so fast that it should have flown apart, unless it held far more mass than we can see.

beats.scene: A spinning disc galaxy with the outer stars moving too fast
beats.summary: In the 1970s Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies and found that the outer stars move as fast as the inner ones, so something unseen must be pulling on them.

beats.scene: Planets drawn on the board with arrows that get shorter farther out
beats.summary: In the solar system, far planets move slowly: the Earth moves at about thirty kilometres a second but Neptune at only about five. Galaxies should work the same way, but they do not.

beats.scene: A glowing galaxy sits inside a huge invisible ball drawn with a dotted line
beats.summary: The simplest explanation is a halo of unseen matter around every galaxy, with about five times as much mass as all the ordinary matter.

beats.scene: A glass of water bends the light of a lamp into a curve
beats.summary: Mass bends light, so a cluster of galaxies acts as a lens and stretches the light of galaxies behind it into arcs; the bending shows that the cluster holds far more mass than we can see.

beats.scene: Two colliding clusters, pink gas in the middle and blue mass beside it
beats.summary: In the Bullet Cluster, two clusters collided: the hot gas was slowed in the middle, but lensing shows that most of the mass passed straight through, so it is not in the gas.

beats.scene: Peaks and dips on a chalk graph of the afterglow's ripple patterns
beats.summary: The pattern of ripples in the afterglow of the Big Bang fits only if dark matter is about five times more plentiful than ordinary matter, which agrees with the galaxies and clusters.

beats.scene: A list: not stars, not gas, not dust, maybe a new particle
beats.summary: Dark matter gives off no light and is not dim stars, gas or dust; it may be a new kind of particle that feels gravity but hardly anything else, such as a WIMP or an axion.

beats.scene: A deep mine shaft leads down to a quiet laboratory with a glowing tank
beats.summary: Experiments hunt for dark matter in deep mines, such as one in South Dakota with a tank of liquid xenon, and in colliders such as the one at CERN; so far nobody has found it.

beats.scene: Two chalk columns: a new particle and a new law of gravity
beats.summary: A few scientists suggest that gravity itself works differently on large scales, an idea called MOND, but it struggles with the Bullet Cluster and the afterglow; most prefer dark matter, and Ravi keeps both on the board.

beats.scene: Anya throws a ball high and watches it slow down as it climbs
beats.summary: Gravity pulls on everything, so astronomers expected the expansion of the universe to be slowing down, like a ball thrown upwards.

beats.scene: A row of exploding stars at different distances, dimmer farther away
beats.summary: To measure the expansion in the past, astronomers used Type Ia supernovae as measuring sticks: their dimness gives distance, and the redshift of their galaxy shows how much space has stretched.

beats.scene: Two teams of astronomers at telescopes on different mountains
beats.summary: In the 1990s two rival teams, led by Saul Perlmutter and by Brian Schmidt, with Adam Riess a key member, hunted for distant supernovae with the biggest telescopes.

beats.scene: A graph where far supernova dots sit dimmer than the expected line
beats.summary: In 1998 both teams found that distant supernovae were fainter than expected, as if they were farther away than they should be.

beats.scene: A car's speedometer needle climbs as the driver presses the pedal
beats.summary: The expansion of the universe is speeding up, like a ball thrown upwards that begins to rise faster; the discovery won the Nobel Prize in 2011.

beats.scene: A pie chart on the board: five, twenty-seven and sixty-eight percent
beats.summary: Dark energy is the name for whatever is speeding up the expansion; with dark matter it makes up about 95 percent of the universe, leaving about five percent for ordinary matter.

beats.scene: The Greek letter lambda, circled twice on the chalkboard
beats.summary: Einstein added a cosmological constant to his equations in 1917 to keep the universe still; after Hubble he is said to have called it his biggest blunder, but it is now the simplest candidate for dark energy.

beats.scene: A chalk number with endless zeros trails off the end of the board
beats.summary: If dark energy is the energy of empty space, quantum theory predicts far too much of it, by a number with more than fifty zeros; this is called the worst prediction in physics.

beats.scene: A balloon grows: the dots of matter thin out, a steady glow stays
beats.summary: Matter thins out as space stretches, but dark energy seems to stay the same; about five billion years ago it won the contest with gravity, and the expansion began to speed up.

beats.scene: A wavy line on a graph bends away from the expected flat line
beats.summary: Recent results from the DESI survey, which mapped millions of galaxies, hint that dark energy may be changing over time; this is not settled and needs more data.

beats.scene: A rocket climbs away from the Earth while a stone falls back
beats.summary: At four o'clock Ravi asks about places where nothing can escape: a rocket needs about eleven kilometres a second to leave the Earth, and in 1783 John Michell imagined a star so heavy that even light could not get out.

beats.scene: An astronomer in uniform writes equations in a notebook beside a trench
beats.summary: Only weeks after Einstein's theory appeared in 1915, Karl Schwarzschild, a soldier in the German army, solved its equations for a round mass and found that a small enough mass would trap even light.

beats.scene: A boat paddles against a river that flows towards a waterfall
beats.summary: A black hole has an edge called the event horizon, a point of no return; at the centre, our theories break down.

beats.scene: A real marble beside a chalk ball six kilometres wide
beats.summary: A black hole forms when a very heavy star collapses; anything could become one if squeezed small enough, the Sun to about six kilometres across and the Earth to the size of a marble.

beats.scene: A tiny chalk Earth circles a black dot where the Sun used to be
beats.summary: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner: if the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would keep orbiting as before, though in the dark.

beats.scene: A tiny astronaut stretched like spaghetti falls towards a dark sphere
beats.summary: Falling into a black hole, you would be stretched like spaghetti by the difference in gravity between your head and your feet, and to a distant watcher you would seem to slow down and freeze at the edge.

beats.scene: Gas streams from a blue star into a glowing disc around an invisible partner
beats.summary: We cannot see a black hole, but gas falling towards one glows brightly in X-rays; in 1971 Cygnus X-1 became the first strong candidate.

beats.scene: Stars whirl in tight orbits around an invisible dark centre
beats.summary: At the heart of the Milky Way the star S2 circles an invisible object every sixteen years; Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez showed that it is a black hole of about four million Suns, and won the Nobel Prize in 2020.

beats.scene: A glowing orange ring around a dark circle, a black hole
beats.summary: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio dishes across the Earth, showed the first picture of a black hole, in the galaxy M87; in 2022 it showed the one at the centre of the Milky Way.

beats.scene: A chain of galaxies with bright points at their centres, growing larger
beats.summary: Almost every large galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its centre, but some already existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang, and how they grew so fast is an open question.

beats.scene: Ravi shakes the edge of the old mattress and ripples run across it
beats.summary: In 1916 Einstein predicted that heavy objects moving through space make ripples in space itself, called gravitational waves, but he doubted anyone could detect them.

beats.scene: Two stars in a tight orbit, with their circle slowly shrinking
beats.summary: In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found two neutron stars whose orbit was shrinking exactly as Einstein's theory predicted if they were losing energy as gravitational waves; they won the Nobel Prize in 1993.

beats.scene: Two long concrete tubes meet at a right angle in an open field
beats.summary: LIGO has two detectors, in Louisiana and Washington State, each with two arms four kilometres long; laser light can measure changes smaller than a thousandth of the width of a proton.

beats.scene: A signal on a screen rises in pitch and ends in a spike
beats.summary: On 14 September 2015 both detectors felt a signal that rose in pitch and faded in a fifth of a second: two black holes had merged more than a billion years earlier.

beats.scene: A tiny spike on a screen inside a huge burst of energy
beats.summary: In that fraction of a second the black holes turned about three Suns' worth of mass into gravitational waves, for a moment more power than all the stars of the visible universe.

beats.scene: Scientists in a conference room cheer around a screen showing the signal
beats.summary: The discovery was announced in February 2016; Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne won the Nobel Prize in 2017, and many more mergers have been detected since.

beats.scene: Two neutron stars spiral together and a burst of light follows moments after
beats.summary: On 17 August 2017 detectors felt ripples from two neutron stars merging about 130 million light-years away; less than two seconds later a flash of gamma rays arrived.

beats.scene: Dozens of telescopes around the world point at one faint glowing spot
beats.summary: Telescopes around the world followed the glow of the crash, called a kilonova, for weeks: it began blue and faded to red as the debris spread and cooled.

beats.scene: A gold ring and a glowing cloud sparkle with flecks of gold
beats.summary: The light of the kilonova showed heavy elements such as gold and platinum, so neutron star collisions are probably a major source of them.

beats.scene: A big ear drawn on the board listens to a spiral of waves
beats.summary: Gravitational waves are a new sense for astronomy, carrying information that light cannot, and a planned space detector called LISA will listen for slower, deeper ripples.

beats.scene: A clock on a mountain top and a clock in a valley, ticking differently
beats.summary: Time runs slightly slower where gravity is stronger; in 1971 clocks flown round the world on airliners ticked differently from clocks on the ground, as Einstein's theory said.

beats.scene: Two tiny glowing atom clocks, one on a shelf and one on the floor
beats.summary: The best atomic clocks can detect time running faster when lifted a few centimetres; astronauts on the space station, moving very fast, age a few thousandths of a second less in six months.

beats.scene: A glowing ball with the Earth at its centre and a dark edge
beats.summary: We can see only the observable universe, because older light has not had time to reach us; as space has stretched while light travelled, its edge is now about 46 billion light-years away, making it about 93 billion light-years wide.

beats.scene: A chalk circle round Anya with galaxies drifting beyond its edge
beats.summary: The edge of the observable universe is not a wall but the limit of sight; every observer has their own, and there is surely more universe beyond it that we cannot see.

beats.scene: Astronauts in a space shuttle bay fit new instruments to a telescope
beats.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 above the blurring air, but its mirror was slightly the wrong shape; in 1993 astronauts fitted corrective optics, like spectacles, and it began to send sharp pictures.

beats.scene: Thousands of tiny galaxies of every shape scattered across black
beats.summary: In 1995 Hubble stared at an apparently empty patch of sky for ten days and found thousands of galaxies, in a patch as small as a grain of sand held at arm's length.

beats.scene: A huge golden mirror made of hexagons floats in space beside a giant sunshield
beats.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on Christmas Day 2021, has a mirror 6 metres wide made of 18 gold-coated segments, and floats about a million and a half kilometres from the Earth behind a sunshield as big as a tennis court.

beats.scene: A cold dark telescope looks through a glowing dust cloud at hidden stars
beats.summary: Webb sees infrared light, which passes through dust and carries the stretched light of the earliest galaxies; to detect faint heat it must itself be colder than minus two hundred degrees.

beats.scene: A huge dome on a desert mountain holds a segmented mirror
beats.summary: On the ground, the Extremely Large Telescope is being built in Chile with a mirror 39 metres wide, and the Square Kilometre Array of radio dishes in Australia and South Africa; both will see far more than today's instruments.

beats.scene: A glowing map of the Milky Way built from a billion tiny dots
beats.summary: The Gaia satellite has measured the positions and motions of nearly two billion stars, making the most exact map of our galaxy.

beats.scene: A lone star with a giant planet very close, drawn in chalk
beats.summary: Until 1995 no planet was known around a Sun-like star; then Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found a giant planet that circles the star 51 Pegasi every four days, and won the Nobel Prize in 2019.

beats.scene: A star wobbles slightly as a hidden planet tugs at it
beats.summary: The planet was found by the wobble of its star: as the planet orbits, it tugs the star to and fro, and the Doppler shift of the starlight reveals the motion.

beats.scene: A star dims slightly as a small dark planet crosses in front
beats.summary: Another method watches for a star to dim as a planet passes in front; the Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, watched about 150,000 stars this way and found thousands of planets.

beats.scene: Strange worlds: a hot giant, a lava world and a planet with two suns
beats.summary: More than five thousand planets around other stars are now known, including hot giants, lava worlds and planets with two suns; most stars seem to have planets, and there are probably billions of Earth-sized ones in our galaxy.

beats.scene: A small red star with seven planets in a row, three of them marked
beats.summary: The habitable zone is the range of distances where a planet could have liquid water; the star TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away, has seven Earth-sized planets, three of them in its zone.

beats.scene: A frozen moon cracks open and a plume of water sprays into space
beats.summary: Liquid water may also lie under the ice of moons in our own solar system, such as Europa and Enceladus, and the Europa Clipper probe is on its way to study Europa.

beats.scene: Starlight passes through a thin ring of air around a planet
beats.summary: When a planet crosses its star, starlight passes through its air and picks up the fingerprints of gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide; no convincing sign of life has been found yet.

beats.scene: A dark rock in a museum case beside drawings of tiny molecules
beats.summary: The ingredients of life are common in space: the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, held more than seventy kinds of amino acids, and similar molecules have been found in gas clouds and asteroid samples.

beats.scene: A single blue Earth on a black cloth, with a question mark beside it
beats.summary: Having the ingredients is not the same as having life: we know of only one world with life, and how it began on Earth is still unknown, though it seems to have started early.

beats.scene: A row of big radio dishes listens to the night sky
beats.summary: Since 1960 scientists have listened for radio signals from other civilisations and heard nothing confirmed; the Wow signal of 1977 never came again, and the puzzle of why we see no one is called the Fermi paradox.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft with a big dish far out in the dark
beats.summary: At five o'clock Ravi turns to distance: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object, more than twenty light-hours away, but it would take about 70,000 years to reach the distance of the nearest star.

beats.scene: A chalk race between a rocket, a space probe and a beam of light
beats.summary: The fastest human-made object, the Parker Solar Probe, reaches about 190 kilometres a second, yet even at that speed a trip to the nearest star would take more than six thousand years.

beats.scene: A tiny chip on a thin silver sail is pushed by a laser beam
beats.summary: One proposal, Breakthrough Starshot, would push tiny probes on light sails with powerful lasers to a fifth of the speed of light, reaching the nearest star in about twenty years; it is only an idea, and the technology does not exist yet.

beats.scene: Space squeezed ahead of a ship and stretched behind it
beats.summary: In 1994 the physicist Miguel Alcubierre showed that Einstein's equations allow a warp bubble that squeezes space ahead and stretches it behind, but it would need a kind of negative energy that nobody knows how to make.

beats.scene: A triangle on a flat sheet, its angles adding up to a line
beats.summary: On the largest scales the universe looks flat: triangles drawn across the afterglow have angles that add up to a straight line, to within a fraction of one percent.

beats.scene: A garden gate opens onto a landscape that never seems to end
beats.summary: Flat does not prove infinite: a flat universe could be finite, like a video game screen that wraps round; we do not know whether the universe is infinite, and we see only a part of it.

beats.scene: A balloon grows in a room while Anya points at the air outside it
beats.summary: The universe need not expand into anything: the expansion only means that distances between galaxies grow, and no outside is needed.

beats.scene: Many soap bubbles, each with a tiny universe inside, float in the air
beats.summary: Some theories suggest that inflation never stops everywhere, so that many bubble universes might exist, but nobody can test this, and some scientists say it is closer to philosophy than science.

beats.scene: A chalk machine with dials set to exact marks
beats.summary: If some physical constants were slightly different, atoms or stars might not work; some take this as a hint of many universes, others as a sign that we do not yet understand why the numbers are what they are.

beats.scene: A tiny pale dot in a beam of sunlight against black space
beats.summary: In 1990, as Voyager 1 left the planets behind, it turned its camera back and photographed the Earth from about six billion kilometres away: a pale dot less than one point of the picture.

beats.scene: A chalk clock face: the Big Bang at one, today at six
beats.summary: Ravi squeezes the history of the universe onto a chalk clock, with the Big Bang at one o'clock and today at six, so that every minute is about 46 million years.

beats.scene: The first stars glimmer near the top of the chalk clock, just after one
beats.summary: On the chalk clock the first stars switch on a few minutes after one, and the first galaxies soon after; then hours pass with no Sun and no Earth.

beats.scene: Chalk hands point to twenty past four beside a swirling disc of gas
beats.summary: At about twenty past four on the clock, a cloud of gas and dust collapses, the Sun lights up, and the planets form from the disc around it, about four and a half billion years ago.

beats.scene: A Mars-sized planet slams into the young Earth in a flash of sparks
beats.summary: Soon afterwards, according to the leading theory, a world about the size of Mars hit the young Earth, and the debris formed the Moon, which may also have tilted the Earth.

beats.scene: Green mats of tiny bacteria spread over a rocky shore under a young Sun
beats.summary: Life appears on the chalk clock at about twenty-three minutes to five, as tiny single cells; the oldest clear fossils, in Australia, are about three and a half billion years old.

beats.scene: Tiny green cells release bubbles of oxygen in a shallow sea
beats.summary: At about ten past five bacteria that used sunlight filled the air with oxygen, in the Great Oxidation; a few minutes later, more complex cells with a nucleus appeared.

beats.scene: Soft sea creatures drift over the sea floor; a tiny plant grows ashore
beats.summary: Animals appear in the sea at about a quarter to six on the chalk clock, and by about ten to six plants and animals have moved onto land.

beats.scene: A dinosaur looks up at a streak of fire in the sky
beats.summary: Dinosaurs rule from about five minutes to six until a minute and a half before six, when an asteroid about ten kilometres wide hits the Earth, 66 million years ago, and ends the reign of nearly all of them; birds are their living descendants.

beats.scene: A tiny sliver at the very end of the chalk clock
beats.summary: Our species appears only about half a second before six; all of recorded history, from the first writing, takes less than a hundredth of a second.

beats.scene: Ravi puts a tiny chalk cross at six o'clock, labelled you are here
beats.summary: Ravi marks a tiny cross at six o'clock and writes you are here; the universe is still very young, because stars will go on being born for trillions of years.

beats.scene: A bright Sun above a dry brown Earth with no oceans
beats.summary: The Sun is slowly getting brighter, and in roughly a billion years it will probably be hot enough to boil away the Earth's oceans.

beats.scene: The Sun swells into a huge red ball over a dry Earth
beats.summary: In about five billion years the Sun will run short of hydrogen and swell into a red giant more than a hundred times wider than now; the inner planets will be scorched or swallowed.

beats.scene: A small white ember glows in the middle of a faint ring of gas
beats.summary: The Sun will then puff off its outer layers and shrink to a white dwarf about the size of the Earth, which will fade and cool for trillions of years.

beats.scene: Two spiral galaxies sweep towards each other along a long curved path
beats.summary: Andromeda is moving towards us at about a hundred kilometres a second, and the two galaxies will probably merge in a few billion years, though new measurements make the timing uncertain.

beats.scene: Distant galaxies fade one by one, leaving a few lights in the dark
beats.summary: Because dark energy speeds up the expansion, galaxies beyond our neighbourhood will move out of sight; in perhaps a hundred billion years the merged local galaxy will be alone in the sky.

beats.scene: A few red lamps in a dark room, going out one by one
beats.summary: New stars will form for a very long time, but the gas is running short; in about a hundred trillion years star formation will stop and the last red dwarfs will burn out.

beats.scene: A thin line drawn on the board leads off to a question mark
beats.summary: If dark energy stays the same, the universe will expand for ever and grow colder, darker and emptier, an ending called the Big Freeze or heat death; but this is the most likely future, not a certain one.

beats.scene: Three chalk arrows on the board: a freeze, a crunch and a rip
beats.summary: Other endings have been suggested: a Big Crunch, where the expansion reverses, and a Big Rip, where dark energy grows stronger and tears everything apart; the evidence does not favour them, but they cannot be ruled out.

beats.scene: A black hole shrinks slowly as faint glowing particles drift away
beats.summary: Even black holes may not last for ever: in 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that they should slowly lose energy and evaporate, though for the biggest this would take a time with about a hundred zeros, and it has not been observed.

beats.scene: Anya writes a very long row of zeros on the board and laughs
beats.summary: None of these endings will affect us; the real lesson is that we live in a rare and lucky moment, when the universe is old enough to have made atoms and planets and young enough to be full of stars.

beats.scene: Ravi writes Known on the left of the board and Unknown on the right
beats.summary: At a quarter to six Ravi wipes the board and writes two columns; under Known go the facts we are sure of, such as the age of the universe and how stars make atoms.

beats.scene: A long list of questions fills the Unknown column, longer than the Known column
beats.summary: Under Unknown go what dark matter and dark energy are, what happened at the very beginning, why matter beat antimatter, and whether there is life elsewhere; the list is longer than the Known list.

beats.scene: Anya holds a magnifying glass over a graph with two lines on it
beats.summary: Scientists test ideas against evidence: a good idea must predict something that could prove it wrong, and then someone must look, as with the eclipse of 1919 and the hiss in the antenna.

beats.scene: Two arrows point to slightly different numbers on a chalk ruler
beats.summary: Sometimes two good methods disagree: the expansion rate measured from nearby supernovae is about nine percent faster than the rate predicted from the early afterglow, a puzzle called the Hubble tension that is still unsolved.

beats.scene: Anya and Ravi shake hands over a board full of chalk crosses
beats.summary: Ravi says that science moves forward when evidence refuses to fit: Mercury's orbit led to Einstein, the hiss led to the Big Bang, and the unsolved puzzles are where the next discoveries wait.

beats.scene: Anya sits under the tree with the empty teapot and a full notebook
beats.summary: It is wonderful that tiny living things on a small planet, with a short time to live, can learn how stars burn and how the whole universe works; Ravi says that in us the universe has found a way to understand itself.

beats.scene: A row of names pinned to the shed door beside the old posters
beats.summary: Ravi shows Anya the names he has pinned beside the posters: Leavitt, Payne, Rubin and Bell, women whose work was not always welcomed at first, and behind them thousands of engineers and students.

beats.scene: A pink sky at sunset with the first bright point shining above the roof
beats.summary: As evening comes, the sky turns pink and the first bright point appears above the roof; Ravi says it is really the planet Venus, and the real stars will follow.

beats.scene: Anya looks up at the darkening sky with her notebook closed in her lap
beats.summary: Anya asks what came before the Big Bang; Ravi says that nobody knows, that scientists have ideas but no proof, and that it might not even be a meaningful question.

beats.scene: The chalkboard is covered with Anya's own new questions in her handwriting
beats.summary: At six o'clock, Anya writes her own questions on the board, and Ravi says that questions are where science begins.
