B1B2: On a hot Sunday, Anya cycled to her uncle Ravi's house with a notebook in her bag. It was one o'clock, and the street was so quiet that she could hear her own bicycle chain.
Ravi was in the garden, carrying a chalkboard on an easel and a huge brown teapot. He put them down under the plum tree, next to a plate of ginger biscuits.
Anya sat down on the grass and asked her uncle a question. She wanted to know what the universe really is, and why nobody ever seems able to explain it in plain words.
Ravi wrote the word “universe” on the board and underlined it twice. He said that it simply means everything that exists, including all of space, all of time, and every bit of matter and energy.
Ravi had only one rule for the afternoon, and he wrote it at the bottom of the board. Ask anything you like, he said, and when nobody knows the answer, we will say so honestly.
Ravi explained that they had five hours, from one o'clock until six. In each stretch of the afternoon they would look at one big idea, and the tea would last the whole way.
Ravi started the ladder of sizes with Anya, who is about a metre and a half tall. Above her he drew a tree, a mountain and the whole Earth, which is about 12,700 kilometres wide.
Next Ravi drew the Sun, a circle so big that the Earth beside it was only a dot. About a million Earths could fit inside the Sun, yet astronomers call it an ordinary star.
Ravi then drew a great spiral of dots, which was the Milky Way. Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in it, and light takes about 100,000 years to cross it.
The Milky Way is only one galaxy among hundreds of billions, and the board was not big enough for the next rung. Ravi laughed, took his chalk to the garden fence and carried on drawing there.
Ravi picked a leaf from the plum tree and gave it to Anya with a magnifying glass. Every leaf is built from tiny living cells, and a cell is far smaller than a grain of sand.
Ravi let a drop of water fall from the garden tap onto Anya's finger. It held more than a billion billion molecules, and each one was made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Atoms are the building blocks of everything, and each atom is mostly empty space. If an atom were as large as a football stadium, its nucleus would be a pea in the middle.
Around the nucleus there are electrons, which are far lighter than the nucleus. They do not circle it like planets, but form a fuzzy cloud, and we can only say where each one is likely to be.
The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, and the number of protons decides what an atom is. One proton makes hydrogen, six make carbon, and seventy-nine make gold.

Protons and neutrons are not the smallest pieces, because each one is built from three even smaller particles called quarks. So far, nobody has found anything inside a quark, although physicists keep looking.
If atoms are empty, why does the table feel hard? Ravi explained that the electrons in Anya's hand push away the electrons in the wood, so her hand never truly touches it.

Ravi wrote the four forces of nature on the board: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong force and the weak force. The last two work only inside atoms, where one holds the nucleus together and the other makes some atoms break down.
Ravi fetched a fridge magnet from the kitchen and held it over a paperclip on the table. The paperclip jumped up to meet it, which showed that a tiny magnet can beat the pull of the entire Earth.
Electric forces can push or pull, and in big objects the pluses and minuses cancel out. Gravity only ever pulls, so every bit adds up, and that is why it rules the large scale.
A ripe plum dropped from the tree and landed beside Anya. Ravi said that Isaac Newton once wondered whether the pull on the plum also holds the Moon in its path.

Ravi drew a cannon on top of a mountain, and the faster it fires, the farther the ball flies before it lands. At the right speed the ball keeps falling around the curve of the Earth without ever reaching the ground.

In 1687 Newton published a law that could predict the pull of gravity between any two objects. The pull grows with their mass and gets weaker as they move apart, so twice as far means four times weaker.
Newton's law worked beautifully, but he knew that it had a gap. He could say how gravity behaves, yet he admitted that he had no idea what gravity actually is.
Ravi dragged an old mattress onto the lawn and lay down in the middle of it. When Anya rolled marbles across it, they curved towards him, which is how Einstein pictured gravity in 1915.
A heavy object bends space, and bent space tells everything nearby how to move. The Earth is not pulled by a rope from the Sun, but follows the straightest path through the curved space around it.
Mercury's orbit slowly turns around the Sun, and Newton's law could not fully explain it. When Einstein worked out the numbers with his new idea, the answer matched what astronomers had seen.

In 1919 there was a total eclipse of the Sun, and astronomers photographed the stars beside it. Their light had been bent by the Sun's gravity, just as Einstein had said, and newspapers around the world reported it.

Satellites high above the Earth carry very exact clocks that tell your phone where it is. Gravity and speed make these clocks run a little differently, and without Einstein's theory your map would soon be wrong by kilometres.
Ravi wrote the word “spacetime” on the board, because space and time bend together. Anya tried to explain it back in her own words, and when she had finished, he clapped.

Ravi switched on a torch and pointed it across the garden, and the light seemed to arrive at once. In fact it travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, enough to go seven and a half times round the Earth.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, so its light needs about eight minutes to reach us. This means that we always see the Sun as it was a little while ago.

Astronomers measure the sky in light-years, which means the distance that light travels in a year. That is about nine and a half trillion kilometres, and the nearest star beyond the Sun is more than four of them away.
On a dark night you can see the Andromeda galaxy as a faint smudge. Its light has travelled for about two and a half million years, so you see it as it was before our species existed.

Anya asked why nothing can go faster than light, and Ravi said that speeding up takes more energy the faster you go. An object with mass can get very close to the speed of light, but it can never quite reach it.

Ravi put a bowl of water on the table and tapped it, and ripples spread across the surface. Light behaves a little like that, but it also arrives in tiny packets called photons, which is one of the oddest facts in physics.
Ravi held a glass prism in the sunshine, and a rainbow appeared on the grass. Newton did the same in 1666, and he showed that white light is a mixture of all the colours.
Ravi shook a long garden hose up and down, and waves ran along it. Slow shakes made long waves and quick shakes made short ones, and in the same way red light has longer waves than blue or violet.
Ravi drew a long line with a tiny rainbow in the middle. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all light too, but our eyes cannot see them.
Ravi told Anya to point her phone's front camera at a television remote and press a button. A purple glow appeared on the screen, which was infrared light that her eyes could not see.
By two o'clock the shadow of the plum tree had moved across the lawn. Ravi drew a rainbow with hundreds of thin dark lines in it, which a German scientist called Fraunhofer had first mapped in 1814.

Ravi sprinkled a pinch of salt onto the flame of his camping stove, and the flame turned bright yellow. Every element has its own pattern of light, so astronomers can read the lines in a star's rainbow like a fingerprint.

In 1868, astronomers saw a yellow line in the Sun's light that matched no element known on Earth. They named the new element helium, after the Greek word for the Sun, and it was only found on Earth in 1895.

In 1925 a young astronomer named Cecilia Payne studied the lines in the light of many stars. She found that they are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, but older experts did not believe her at first.
An ambulance went past the garden gate, and its siren sounded high as it came and low as it left. This is called the Doppler effect, and the Austrian Christian Doppler explained it in 1842.

Light is stretched in the same way when its source moves away from us, so it looks redder. Astronomers measure how far the dark lines have shifted towards red, and from that shift they can work out the speed of the star.

Ravi held up a thumb at arm's length and closed one eye and then the other, and the thumb seemed to jump. In the same way, nearby stars seem to shift as the Earth circles the Sun, and the shift tells us their distance.

Henrietta Leavitt worked at Harvard, studying thousands of photographs of the sky. She found that certain stars rise and fall in brightness, and the brighter ones do so more slowly, which lets us measure distance.
In 1923 an astronomer named Edwin Hubble found one of Leavitt's pulsing stars inside the Andromeda smudge. Its distance was so great that Andromeda had to be another galaxy, far outside our own.

Hubble then measured the redshifts of many galaxies and found that almost all of them are moving away from us. The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves, so a galaxy twice as far away moves twice as fast.
Anya asked whether this meant that we are at the centre of everything. Ravi fetched a bowl of dough with raisins in it, and as it rose, every raisin moved away from every other raisin.
As the balloon grew, the dots moved apart and none of them was at the centre. The galaxies are not flying through space, said Ravi, because space itself is stretching.
Ravi told Anya to imagine running the film backwards. The galaxies would move closer and closer, until, nearly fourteen billion years ago, everything was squeezed into a hot, dense mass.

The Big Bang was not an explosion in one place, but a stretching of space everywhere at once. A Belgian priest and scientist named Georges Lemaître first suggested the idea, and the name was invented by a rival on the radio.

Hoyle preferred an idea called the Steady State, in which the universe had always looked the same. However, in 1948 Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman calculated that a faint glow from the hot beginning should still fill the sky.
Two engineers named Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson were testing a big horn-shaped antenna in New Jersey. They kept hearing a faint hiss, and it came from every direction in the sky, day and night.

The engineers even removed two pigeons that had been nesting in the antenna, and they scrubbed away the droppings. The hiss stayed exactly the same, until a friend put them in touch with a team at Princeton University.

The hiss was very old light, which first spread through the universe about 380,000 years after the beginning. The expansion has stretched it ever since, until it became microwaves only a few degrees above absolute zero.
Ravi had an old television in the shed, and he switched it on with no channel tuned in. A small part of the snowy static on the screen, he said, was the afterglow of the Big Bang.

Three satellites named COBE, WMAP and Planck have drawn maps of the whole sky in this ancient light. The glow is almost perfectly even, but tiny patches of warmer and cooler light show where the first galaxies would later form.
Ravi drew a long timeline and put a question mark at its left end. Scientists can follow the story back to a tiny fraction of a second, but at the very first instant our theories stop working.

In 1980 a physicist named Alan Guth suggested that the young universe grew enormously fast in a tiny fraction of a second. This idea, called inflation, would explain why the universe is so smooth, but it has not yet been proved.

In the first second, the universe was a hot soup, far hotter than the middle of any star. Ravi wrote Einstein's famous equation on the board, which shows that energy can turn into matter and matter into energy.

As the young universe expanded, it cooled, and within about a millionth of a second the quarks joined in threes. They made protons and neutrons, the building blocks of every nucleus that exists today.
Energy makes particles in pairs, and every particle has a twin called an antiparticle. When the two meet they vanish in a flash of light, which is why antimatter is so hard to keep.

If matter and antimatter had been exactly equal, everything would have vanished. But for roughly every billion pairs, one extra particle of matter survived, and the stars, the Earth and Anya are made of those leftovers.
A few minutes after the start, the universe was still hot enough for protons and neutrons to stick together. They formed the nuclei of helium, and the whole cooking lasted only about twenty minutes.
The universe came out of this cooking with about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium. It then became too cool and too thin for more fusion, so heavier atoms had to wait for the stars.

For about 380,000 years the universe was a hot fog of charged particles, and light kept bumping into them. When it cooled to about three thousand degrees, atoms formed, the fog cleared, and the light flew free.
After the light escaped, the universe went dark, because there were no stars yet. Slowly, gravity pulled the gas towards the slightly denser patches, and the rich patches grew richer.

The first stars switched on perhaps a hundred or two hundred million years after the Big Bang. The Webb telescope has since seen galaxies from less than 300 million years after the start, and some are brighter than scientists expected.
Anya pumped up her bicycle tyre, and the pump grew warm in her hand. A collapsing cloud of gas heats up in the same way, and its centre becomes so hot that hydrogen begins to fuse.

In the core of the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus, and a tiny part of the mass turns into energy. Every second the Sun changes about four million tonnes of its own mass into light and heat.
Ravi explained that every steady star is a balance between two great forces. Gravity squeezes it inwards, while the heat from fusion pushes outwards, and the balance can last for billions of years.

Light made in the middle of the Sun cannot travel straight out, because the gas is so dense. It bounces from atom to atom for many thousands of years, and then it crosses space to the Earth in only eight minutes.

How long a star lives depends on how heavy it is, and the heaviest stars live the shortest lives. The biggest burn their fuel in only a few million years, but small red dwarfs can shine for trillions of years.
When the hydrogen in its core runs out, a star swells into a red giant. The core grows hotter, and helium atoms begin to fuse into carbon and oxygen.
Ravi cut an onion in half to show the layers inside it. A very heavy star is built like that, with layers of lighter elements on the outside and a core of iron at the centre.
Fusing iron takes in energy instead of giving it out, so the star's engine stops. The core collapses in less than a second, and the whole star blows apart in an explosion called a supernova.

In 1054, astronomers in China recorded a bright new star in the sky, and its remains are now called the Crab Nebula. In 1987 a supernova in a nearby galaxy sent ghostly particles called neutrinos, which were detected hours before its light was seen.
At three o'clock Ravi made a fresh pot of tea and turned to the smaller stars. A star like our Sun does not explode, but puffs its outer layers into a glowing cloud and leaves a white dwarf.

Some white dwarfs circle close to another star, and they steal its gas until they explode. Because these explosions are always about equally bright, astronomers use them like pulsing stars to measure distances.
Sometimes the collapsed core of a heavy star survives as a neutron star, only about twenty kilometres wide. It is heavier than the Sun, so a single teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.

In 1967 a student named Jocelyn Bell found a radio signal that pulsed regularly, about once every second and a third. It was so regular that her team half-joked that it came from aliens, but it was really a spinning neutron star.

The gas thrown out by dying stars mixes with clouds of hydrogen and makes new stars. Our Sun was born about four and a half billion years ago from a cloud that already contained atoms made by older stars.
The first stars were made only of hydrogen and helium, so they probably had no rocky planets. Rock and metal, water and air all need heavier elements, and those had to be made by earlier stars first.
Ravi pinned a colourful poster of the elements to the shed door. Each square was coloured to show where the element was made, such as the Big Bang, a dying star, or an exploding star.
Anya held up her hand and looked at it as if she had never seen it before. Most of her atoms are hydrogen from the Big Bang, while the carbon and the iron in her blood were made in stars.
Ravi said that the hydrogen atoms in Anya's body are nearly as old as the universe itself. They have been part of many other things, and one day they will be part of others again.

New stars are still being born today, and the Orion Nebula is a good place to look for them. This cloud of glowing gas is about 1,300 light-years away, and on a winter night you can see it as a faint blur.
Gravity gathered the stars into great islands called galaxies. Some are spirals like a whirlpool, some are round or oval, and some are small and untidy.
Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral with a bar of stars across its middle. The Sun is about 26,000 light-years from the centre, in a quiet part of one of the arms.
On a dark night we see the Milky Way as a pale band across the sky. In 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at it and saw that it is made of countless faint stars.

The Sun is moving at about 200 kilometres a second round the centre of the galaxy. Even at that speed one orbit takes about 230 million years, so the last time it was here, the first dinosaurs were appearing.
Two small galaxies called the Magellanic Clouds circle our own, and people in the south can see them with the naked eye. The Large Cloud is where the supernova of 1987 exploded.
The Milky Way belongs to a family of galaxies called the Local Group. Andromeda is the biggest member, and there are dozens of small ones, spread across about ten million light-years.
Groups of galaxies gather into even bigger families called clusters. The Virgo Cluster, about 55 million light-years away, contains more than a thousand galaxies, all held together by gravity.
On the largest scale, galaxies are arranged in long threads and sheets around enormous empty voids. The result looks like soap foam or a sponge, and astronomers call it the cosmic web.
Astronomers think that there are hundreds of billions of galaxies that we can see, and perhaps many more. Many hold billions of stars, and yet most of space is almost completely empty.

Galaxies sometimes crash into each other, and the crash can last for hundreds of millions of years. But the stars are so far apart that almost none of them touch, like tennis balls in a huge car park.

In 1933 an astronomer named Fritz Zwicky studied a cluster of galaxies and found that they moved far too fast. The cluster should have flown apart, so he guessed that there was a lot of unseen matter holding it together.

In the 1970s an astronomer named Vera Rubin measured how fast the stars in spiral galaxies are moving. The stars at the edges were going as fast as those near the centre, which should not happen unless there is hidden mass.
In our solar system, the planets far from the Sun move slowly. Neptune travels at about five kilometres a second, while the Earth speeds along at about thirty.
The simplest explanation is that each galaxy sits inside a huge, invisible halo. This dark matter has about five times as much mass as all the ordinary matter put together.

Ravi held up a glass of water, and the light of a lamp behind it bent into a curve. In the same way, a cluster of galaxies bends the light behind it into arcs, and the bending shows how much mass it has.

In the Bullet Cluster, two clusters of galaxies have crashed into each other. The hot gas stayed behind in the middle, but the mass measured by lensing carried straight on, so most of it cannot be gas.

Another clue is the ripple pattern in the afterglow of the Big Bang. The pattern can only be explained if there is about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter, which agrees with the galaxies.
Dark matter gives off no light, so it is not made of stars, gas or dust. Many scientists think that it is a new kind of particle that feels gravity but almost nothing else.
Scientists look for dark matter in deep mines, where the rock blocks other rays. In a mine in South Dakota a big tank of liquid xenon waits for a tiny flash, but so far nobody has seen one.

A few scientists suggest that gravity itself works differently on huge scales, an idea called MOND. It struggles to explain colliding clusters and the afterglow, so most scientists prefer dark matter.
Anya threw a ball into the air and watched it slow down as it climbed. Gravity pulls on everything in the universe too, so astronomers expected the expansion to be slowing down.
To find out, astronomers needed to measure the expansion in the distant past. They used Type Ia supernovae, which are always about equally bright, so how dim one looks shows how far away it is.
In the 1990s two teams of astronomers hunted for distant supernovae. One was led by Saul Perlmutter and the other by Brian Schmidt, and each used the biggest telescopes in the world.
In 1998 both teams of astronomers found the very same surprise in their results. The distant supernovae looked fainter than expected, so they were farther away than they should have been.
The only explanation was that the expansion of the universe is speeding up. It was as if a ball thrown into the air had started to rise faster, and the discovery won the Nobel Prize in 2011.
Scientists call whatever is speeding up the expansion dark energy. Ravi drew a circle on the board, and it showed that ordinary matter is only about five percent of the universe.

In 1917 Einstein added a term called the cosmological constant to his equations, to stop the universe from changing. After Hubble's discovery he is said to have called it his biggest mistake, yet it may be the answer.
Some scientists think that dark energy is the energy of empty space itself. But when physicists calculate it using quantum theory, the answer is far too big, and nobody knows why.

As space stretches, the matter in it spreads thinner, but dark energy seems to stay just as strong. Because of this, dark energy took the lead about five billion years ago, and the expansion has been speeding up ever since.

In recent years, a survey called DESI has mapped the positions of millions of galaxies. Its results hint that dark energy may be getting weaker with time, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to be sure.

At four o'clock Ravi explained that a rocket must reach about eleven kilometres a second to leave the Earth. In 1783 John Michell, a clergyman, imagined a star so heavy that even light could not escape from it.

A German astronomer named Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations for a round object only weeks after they appeared. He did the sums as a soldier in the First World War, and they showed that a very small, heavy object could trap even light.
Ravi drew a boat on a river that was heading for a waterfall. A black hole has a point of no return called the event horizon, and nothing that crosses it can escape.

Black holes form when very heavy stars collapse, and any object could become one if it were squeezed small enough. The Sun would need to shrink to a ball about six kilometres across, and the Earth to the size of a marble.
Black holes are often described as cosmic vacuum cleaners, but that is wrong. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would go on orbiting just as before, in the dark.

Near a black hole, gravity pulls harder on your feet than on your head, so a falling astronaut would be stretched like spaghetti. To a watcher far away, the astronaut would seem to slow down and freeze at the edge.
A black hole itself is dark, but the gas falling towards it gets so hot that it shines in X-rays. In 1971 a source of X-rays called Cygnus X-1 became the first strong candidate for a black hole.
At the centre of the Milky Way, stars race round something invisible. One star circles it every sixteen years, and these orbits show that it has about four million times the mass of the Sun.

In 2019 a network of radio telescopes across the Earth, called the Event Horizon Telescope, showed the first picture of a black hole. It is a dark circle inside a glowing ring of hot gas, in a galaxy 55 million light-years away.
Almost every large galaxy seems to have a giant black hole in its centre. Some of them already existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang, and how they grew so fast is still a puzzle.
Ravi shook the old mattress, and ripples ran across its surface. In 1916 Einstein predicted that moving heavy objects make ripples in space itself, but he doubted anyone could detect them.

In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found two neutron stars circling closely round each other. Their orbit was shrinking at exactly the rate that Einstein's theory predicted, which was strong indirect evidence for gravitational waves.

To catch a gravitational wave, scientists built two detectors called LIGO, one in Louisiana and one in Washington State. Each has two arms four kilometres long, and laser light can measure changes smaller than a thousandth of the width of a proton.

On 14 September 2015 both detectors felt a short signal that rose in pitch like a chirp. It came from two black holes, each about thirty times the mass of the Sun, which had crashed together more than a billion years earlier.
In that fraction of a second, the black holes turned the mass of about three Suns into waves. For a moment the power was greater than that of all the stars in the visible universe put together.
Scientists checked the signal for months, and they announced it in February 2016. Three leaders of the project won the Nobel Prize in 2017, and since then detectors have heard many more crashes.

On 17 August 2017 detectors felt the ripples of two neutron stars crashing together, about 130 million light-years away. Less than two seconds later, space telescopes saw a flash of gamma rays from the same place.
Hundreds of astronomers and dozens of telescopes studied the glow in the weeks that followed. It began bright and blue, and then it faded to red as the cloud of debris spread out and cooled.

The light of the crash showed that it had made heavy elements such as gold and platinum. This suggests that crashes of neutron stars are an important source of the gold on Earth, though other sources may exist.

Until 2015 astronomy used only light and other waves of the same family. Gravitational waves are a completely new sense, and a space detector called LISA is planned to listen for even slower ripples in the 2030s.

Einstein's theory says that time runs more slowly where gravity is stronger. In 1971 scientists flew very exact clocks round the world on airliners, and the clocks ticked slightly differently from those on the ground.

Modern atomic clocks are so exact that they can notice time running faster when they are lifted by just a few centimetres. Astronauts on the space station, who move very fast, age a few thousandths of a second less in six months.

The universe is about fourteen billion years old, so light from farther away has not reached us yet. But space has stretched while the light was travelling, so the edge of what we can see is now about 46 billion light-years away.
The edge of the observable universe is not a wall, but only the limit of what light has had time to show us. Someone living in a faraway galaxy would have their own limit, centred on them.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 to see above the blurring air. Its mirror turned out to be slightly the wrong shape, so in 1993 astronauts fitted it with a kind of spectacles.

In 1995 astronomers pointed Hubble at an apparently empty patch of sky for ten days. The patch was as small as a grain of sand held at arm's length, and the picture showed about three thousand galaxies.

The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on Christmas Day in 2021, and its mirror is made of eighteen golden hexagons. It floats about one and a half million kilometres from the Earth, behind a sunshield as big as a tennis court.

Webb looks at infrared light, which can pass through dust and which carries the stretched light of the earliest galaxies. To see such faint heat, the telescope itself must be colder than minus two hundred degrees.

On the ground, astronomers are building the Extremely Large Telescope in Chile, with a mirror 39 metres wide. In Australia and South Africa they are also putting up thousands of radio dishes, called the Square Kilometre Array.
A satellite called Gaia has measured the exact positions and movements of nearly two billion stars. It has made the most detailed map of the Milky Way that has ever been drawn.
Until 1995 nobody had found a planet around a star like our Sun. Then two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, found a giant planet that circles its star in only four days.
A planet tugs its star a little as it circles, so the star wobbles back and forth. The Doppler shift in the star's light, which Ravi had explained earlier, reveals this movement.

Another method is to watch for a star to dim slightly as a planet crosses in front of it. The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, watched about 150,000 stars in this way and found thousands of planets.
More than five thousand planets around other stars are now known, and they are very varied. Some are giant balls of gas that orbit very close to their stars, and some are worlds of molten rock.

A planet can have liquid water if it is neither too close to its star nor too far away. A small red star called TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years from us, has seven Earth-sized planets, and three of them lie in this zone.
Liquid water may also exist closer to home, hidden under the ice of moons such as Europa and Enceladus. A spacecraft called Europa Clipper is on its way to Jupiter to study the ocean of Europa.

When a planet crosses in front of its star, some of the starlight passes through the planet's air. The gases leave dark lines in the light, like the fingerprints in a star's rainbow, and Webb can read them.
In 1969 a meteorite fell near a town called Murchison in Australia. It contained more than seventy kinds of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.
Having the ingredients is not the same as having life. We know of only one world where life exists, and nobody knows exactly how it began there.
Since 1960 scientists have listened with radio telescopes for messages from other civilisations. They have heard nothing certain, and the strange Wow signal of 1977 has never come again.
