They clumped together in threes, said Ravi, forming the first protons and neutrons, which are the building blocks of every nucleus that has ever existed. Anya pointed out that a millionth of a second sounded like a very short time for such a big event, and Ravi agreed that the early universe was in a tremendous hurry.

Whenever energy turns into a particle, said Ravi, it makes a pair: the particle and its mirror-image twin, which is called antimatter. An American physicist named Carl Anderson found the first antiparticle, the positron, in 1932, and when matter and antimatter meet, both vanish in a flash of energy. The early universe, therefore, was full of pairs appearing and disappearing, like sparks flying from a fire.

If matter and antimatter had been made in exactly equal amounts, they would have wiped each other out, and the universe would now contain nothing but light. Instead, for roughly every billion pairs, one extra particle of matter survived, and every star, planet and person is made from those leftovers. Physicists are still searching for the reason, said Ravi, and Anya wrote it in her notebook as one of the biggest unsolved puzzles she had ever heard.

Then came the first great cooking session, said Ravi, which began within the first few minutes, when the universe was still hot enough for protons and neutrons to stick together. They fused into the nuclei of helium, along with tiny amounts of hydrogen's heavier cousins and a trace of lithium, and the whole process was over in about twenty minutes. Anya remarked that most recipes take a good deal longer, and Ravi replied that most ovens are not the size of the universe.

When the cooking ended, the universe was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass, and that is still almost exactly what the oldest stars contain. Expansion had made it too cool and too thin for any more fusion, so the heavier elements, such as carbon and iron, would have to wait for stars to make them. The match between this recipe and what astronomers measure, Ravi said, is one of the strongest proofs that the Big Bang really happened.

For the first 380,000 years, said Ravi, the universe was filled with a glowing fog of electrons and nuclei, and light could not travel far before it bumped into something and was scattered. When the temperature fell to about three thousand degrees, the electrons settled onto the nuclei to make the first true atoms, and the fog suddenly cleared. That was the moment when the radio hiss was set free, and it has been travelling towards us ever since.

After the afterglow faded from view, the universe entered what astronomers call the dark ages, for there were no stars yet and nothing but cooling gas to shine. Gravity went quietly to work on the slightly denser patches that the satellites had mapped, drawing in more and more gas, so that the rich patches grew richer and the thin regions grew thinner. It would take a few hundred million years for the first clump to become hot enough to ignite, and Ravi poured himself another cup of tea while he waited.

Towards three o'clock, said Ravi, the lamps of the universe began to come on, as the first stars lit up perhaps a hundred or two hundred million years after the Big Bang. Nobody has yet seen one of those very first stars directly, but the Webb space telescope has photographed whole galaxies as they were less than 300 million years after the beginning. Some of them are brighter and more mature than anyone expected, and astronomers are busy arguing about what that means.

Ravi sent Anya to fetch her bicycle pump, and he asked her to inflate the tyre as fast as she could and then touch the barrel of the pump. It was surprisingly warm, because squeezing a gas heats it, and the same thing happens when gravity squeezes a great cloud of gas into a ball. At about ten million degrees in its centre, the ball of gas becomes hot enough for the hydrogen nuclei to crash together and fuse, and a star is born.

Inside the Sun, said Ravi, four hydrogen nuclei are squeezed together to make one helium nucleus, and the new nucleus weighs very slightly less than the four that went into it. The missing mass has not vanished but has turned into energy, exactly as Einstein's equation says it should, and every second the Sun converts about four million tonnes of itself into light and heat. Even so, the Sun is so enormous that it has lost only a tiny fraction of its mass in nearly five billion years of shining.

Ravi picked up the balloon again and squeezed it gently in both hands, so that the air inside pushed back. A star is held in shape in much the same way, he said, with gravity squeezing it inwards and the heat of fusion pushing it outwards. The two forces are so well matched that the Sun has stayed almost exactly the same size for billions of years, a patient argument that has not yet been settled.

The energy made in the Sun's core cannot simply stream out, because the gas there is so dense that light is absorbed and sent out again and again, wandering in random directions like a lost traveller in a maze. It can take many thousands of years to reach the surface, yet the final leg across empty space to the Earth takes only about eight minutes. The warmth on Anya's face, therefore, was the work of the Sun long before there were any cities on Earth.

It may seem odd, Ravi said, but the heaviest stars have the shortest lives, because the enormous pressure at their centres makes them burn their fuel at a furious rate. A giant star may blaze for only a few million years, while a small, dim red dwarf sips its hydrogen so slowly that it could shine for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed so far. Our Sun, in between, has a lifetime of about ten billion years, and it is about halfway through.

Eventually, Ravi said, the hydrogen in a star's core runs out, and the star's outer layers swell until it becomes a red giant, many times wider than before. At the same time its core contracts and grows hotter, until helium nuclei begin to fuse into carbon and oxygen, the elements that make up so much of living things. A star, he told Anya, is a kitchen where the lightest ingredients are cooked into heavier ones.

Ravi fetched an onion from the kitchen, sliced it in half and held it up beside his chalk drawing of a heavy star. Such a star, he explained, goes on cooking heavier and heavier elements in its centre until it has layers like the onion, from hydrogen outside to a core of iron. Anya, whose eyes were stinging, said that she was not sure whether it was the onion or the astrophysics.

Iron is the end of the line, said Ravi, because fusing it takes in energy instead of giving it out, so the star's furnace suddenly has nothing left to burn. Within a second the core collapses under its own weight, and the rest of the star is blasted into space in a supernova, which for a few weeks can shine as brightly as an entire galaxy. Anya stared at the board and said that a fact that violent ought to come with a drum roll.

In the year 1054, astronomers in China wrote that a guest star had appeared in the sky, bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks, and its glowing remains can still be seen through a telescope as the Crab Nebula. In 1987 a star exploded in a neighbouring galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and detectors deep underground caught a burst of ghostly particles called neutrinos a few hours before the first flash of light. Neutrinos pass through almost everything, Ravi added, and billions from the Sun were crossing every thumbnail in the garden each second, so Anya moved her thumb out of the way, just in case.

By three o'clock the shadows had grown long enough to reach the fence, and Ravi made a fresh pot of tea before turning to the smaller stars. A star like our Sun, he said, does not explode at the end of its life, but gently puffs its outer layers into space as a glowing shell of gas. What is left at the centre is a white dwarf, a hot ember about as big as the Earth, and a teaspoon of it would weigh about as much as an elephant.

Some white dwarfs have a companion star so close that they pull gas from it, and the ember slowly grows heavier until it passes a critical weight. Then it explodes in what is called a Type Ia supernova, which is always of very nearly the same brightness, so that astronomers can use it, like Leavitt's pulsing stars, as a measuring stick across enormous distances. Ravi tapped the board and told Anya to remember these explosions, because they would return to the story later in the afternoon.

Sometimes the core that is left behind by a supernova does not collapse any further, and it survives as a neutron star, a ball of neutrons squeezed together until it is only about twenty kilometres across. Such a ball is as wide as a small city, yet it contains more mass than the Sun, so that a single teaspoon of its material would weigh several billion tonnes. Anya looked at the teaspoon in her own cup and decided that she would never again complain about the weight of anything.

In 1967 a young research student named Jocelyn Bell, who was working on a new radio telescope in England, found a signal that pulsed with astonishing regularity, about once every second and a third. The pulses were so precise that her team half-jokingly labelled the source LGM, for little green men, before realising that it was a neutron star spinning like a lighthouse. Such objects are now called pulsars, and thousands of them are known, some spinning hundreds of times a second, each sweeping a beam of radio waves past the Earth with every turn.

Nothing in the universe is wasted, said Ravi, because the gas thrown out by dying stars drifts into great clouds, mixes with the hydrogen already there, and eventually collapses to form new stars. Our Sun was born in this way about four and a half billion years ago, from a cloud already seasoned with carbon, oxygen and iron that had been cooked in earlier generations of stars. In a sense, he added, the Sun is a second-hand star, and so is everything that orbits it.

The very first stars, which were made of nothing but hydrogen and helium, could probably not have had planets like ours, said Ravi, since a rocky world needs silicon, oxygen, iron and many other heavier elements. Those had to be forged first inside stars and scattered by their explosions, so the Earth, with its rocks and oceans and air, could only appear after at least one generation of stars had lived and died. Anya looked down at the lawn beneath her feet, and for the first time she saw it as the product of a very long history.

Ravi pinned a large poster of the periodic table to the shed door, and Anya saw that each square was coloured according to where its element had been made. Hydrogen came mostly from the Big Bang, carbon from the winds of dying stars, oxygen from the explosions of heavy ones, and iron from exploding stars of several kinds. The origin of a few of the very heaviest elements, he admitted, was still marked with question marks, because astronomers had not yet settled where they came from.

Anya held up her hand and looked at it as though she had never seen it before. Most of the atoms in it, Ravi told her, are hydrogen from the Big Bang, but the carbon in her cells, the calcium in her bones and the iron in her blood were forged in stars. She was made, he said, not merely of stardust but of the ashes of several generations of stars, and Anya spent a moment thinking about that in silence.

The hydrogen in her body, Ravi went on, is almost as old as the universe itself, having been made in the first moments and never destroyed since. Atoms are not owned by anybody, but only borrowed, and the ones in Anya's hand had probably been part of rivers, rocks and clouds before they were part of her. In time, he said gently, they would be lent to something else, and the universe would hardly notice the change.

The recycling has not stopped, said Ravi, and new stars are being born at this very moment, for example in the Orion Nebula, a glowing cloud about 1,300 light-years away. On a clear winter night you can find it with the naked eye as a faint blur in the sword of the hunter Orion, and through a telescope it becomes a nursery of young stars. Anya made a note to look for it in December, and to remember that she would be looking at a place very like the one where the Sun was born.

Over hundreds of millions of years, said Ravi, gravity gathered the stars into enormous islands called galaxies, and it did not make them all alike. Some are graceful spirals, like a whirlpool of light, others are smooth ovals of old red stars, and others are small and ragged, with no clear shape at all. Anya copied the three sketches into her notebook and gave each of them a nickname.

Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral with a bar of stars across its middle, Ravi said, and he drew it carefully with its long, curving arms. The Sun sits about 26,000 light-years from the centre, in a quiet and unremarkable stretch of one of those arms, which is probably just as well for the planets nearby. The crowded centre of a galaxy, he explained, may be a more dangerous place, because the stars are closer together and the explosions are more frequent.

On a dark night, said Ravi, you can see our galaxy as a pale band arching across the sky, and you are really looking along its flat disc from the inside. The ancient Greeks called it a milky circle, but in 1610 Galileo turned his new telescope towards it and saw that the milk was made of countless faint stars. Anya promised herself that she would find somewhere properly dark to look at it, far away from the street lights.

The Sun is not standing still, said Ravi, but is sweeping round the centre of the galaxy at about 200 kilometres a second, carrying the whole solar system with it. Even at that speed one orbit takes some 230 million years, so the last time the Sun was at this point in its journey, the first dinosaurs were only just beginning to appear. Anya did a quick calculation and discovered that the Sun has completed only about twenty laps since it was born.

Not all galaxies are giants, said Ravi, and two small ones, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, circle the Milky Way like faithful dogs. They look like detached pieces of the Milky Way to anyone in the southern half of the world, where they can be seen with the naked eye, and people have watched them for thousands of years. The Large Cloud is also where the supernova of 1987 exploded, so Anya was already acquainted with it.

The Milky Way is not alone, said Ravi, but belongs to a small family called the Local Group, which includes the giant Andromeda galaxy, a middle-sized spiral called Triangulum and dozens of dwarf galaxies. The whole family is spread across about ten million light-years, and gravity holds its members together even while the space between other galaxies grows. In other words, he said with a grin, the expansion of the universe stops at the garden gate.

Groups of galaxies gather into bigger families called clusters, which may hold thousands of galaxies bound together by their own gravity. The nearest big one, the Virgo Cluster, lies about 55 million light-years away and contains more than a thousand galaxies, and its pull is one of the reasons why our own corner of space is being tugged a little towards it. Ravi drew it on the board as a tight bundle of dots and then ran out of room for the next level.

On the very largest scale, said Ravi, galaxies are strung along vast threads and sheets that surround enormous voids where there are hardly any galaxies at all. The result looks like a sponge or a froth of soap bubbles, and astronomers call it the cosmic web, the largest structure that we know. In 2014 astronomers mapped the great region that contains the Milky Way and gave it a Hawaiian name, Laniakea, which means immense heaven.

Counting is hard, said Ravi, but astronomers estimate that there are at least a few hundred billion galaxies in the part of the universe that we can observe, and some estimates run into trillions. Many of them hold hundreds of billions of stars, so the total number of stars is far greater than the number of grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth. And yet, he added, most of space is almost perfectly empty, with galaxies like tiny lamps scattered across an immense darkness.

Galaxies do sometimes collide, said Ravi, and the encounters last for hundreds of millions of years while gravity stretches each galaxy into long streamers of stars and gas. Strangely, almost no stars actually hit one another, because the distances between stars are so enormous that two galaxies passing through each other are like two swarms of tennis balls drifting through a pair of car parks. The tangle that results can make new stars by the million, and the galaxies slowly join into one.

The trouble began in 1933, when a Swiss astronomer named Fritz Zwicky studied a cluster of galaxies in the constellation Coma and found that its members were moving much too fast. The visible matter did not have nearly enough gravity to hold them, he calculated, and the cluster ought to have flown apart long ago. He concluded that there must be a great deal of unseen matter, which he called dark matter, but few people took him seriously for decades.

In the 1970s an American astronomer named Vera Rubin, working with her colleague Kent Ford, measured how fast the stars in spiral galaxies move round their centres. To everyone's surprise, the stars at the edges moved just as fast as those near the middle, which should only happen if there is a great deal of hidden mass spread through the galaxy and far beyond its visible edge. Rubin went on to check galaxy after galaxy, and to her growing astonishment every one of them told the very same story.

To see why this was so strange, Ravi drew the planets on the board with an arrow for each one, and the arrows grew shorter the farther the planet was from the Sun. The Earth travels at about thirty kilometres a second, while distant Neptune moves at barely five, because the Sun's pull weakens with distance. If most of a galaxy's mass were in its bright centre, the outer stars ought to behave like Neptune, but they do not.

The simplest explanation, said Ravi, is that every galaxy sits in the middle of an enormous invisible halo, whose gravity speeds up the outer stars. Altogether this dark matter seems to outweigh all the ordinary matter, the stuff of stars and planets and people, by about five to one. Anya said that it made the whole bright universe look like the froth on top of a very large cup of tea.

Ravi held a glass of water in front of a lamp, and the light behind it was bent into a smeared curve. Gravity bends light in the same way, as Einstein had said, so the biggest clusters of galaxies act as huge lenses that stretch the light from galaxies far behind them into ghostly arcs. The amount of bending reveals how much mass the cluster really has, and it is always several times more than the stars and gas can account for.

In 2006 astronomers studied a pair of galaxy clusters that had crashed into each other, called the Bullet Cluster, and they found something that was hard to explain without dark matter. The hot gas, which makes up most of the ordinary matter, had been slowed down and left in a heap in the middle. But the lensing showed that most of the mass had sailed straight through and out the other side, because dark matter, it seemed, hardly notices anything, not even itself.

A different line of evidence comes from the afterglow of the Big Bang, said Ravi, because the pattern of its ripples depends on what the early universe was made of. The satellites found that the pattern fits only if dark matter is about five times more plentiful than ordinary matter, exactly the proportion that the spinning galaxies and the colliding clusters had pointed to. When three entirely different methods agree, he said, scientists begin to sit up and take notice.

Whatever dark matter is, said Ravi, it is not stars or gas or dust, because all of those would glow or block the light behind them, and it is probably not mostly black holes either. Most physicists suspect that it is a new kind of particle, perhaps a heavy one that has been given the name WIMP, or a very light one called the axion, that feels gravity but almost nothing else. The truth is that nobody knows, and Anya found that there was a certain comfort in hearing a teacher say so.

To catch a dark matter particle, scientists have built detectors in deep mines, where the rock above blocks almost everything else. One in South Dakota holds a tank of liquid xenon that waits for a single tiny flash, and others try to make dark matter in colliders such as the one at CERN near Geneva. So far nobody has found a trace, which Ravi cheerfully described as the most expensive silence in the history of science.

In 1983 an Israeli physicist named Mordehai Milgrom suggested a different answer, which was that gravity itself might behave differently at very large scales, so that no dark matter would be needed. That idea, called MOND, explains the spinning galaxies rather well, but it struggles with the colliding clusters and the afterglow, and so most scientists still prefer dark matter. Ravi kept both ideas on the board, because a good scientist, he said, never throws away a rival before the evidence has finished speaking.

Anya threw a ball high into the air and watched it slow down as it climbed, because gravity was pulling it back towards the Earth. Gravity is pulling on every galaxy in the same way, Ravi pointed out, so for most of the twentieth century astronomers expected the expansion of the universe to be slowing down. The only question that remained was whether it would slow so much that it would one day stop and fall back.

To find out, astronomers needed a way to measure the expansion at different times in the past, and Ravi reminded Anya of the Type Ia supernovae from earlier. Because each of these explosions has almost the same true brightness, how dim one looks tells us its distance, and the redshift of its galaxy tells us how much the universe has stretched while the light was travelling. Put the two together, and you can watch the history of the expansion unfold.

In the 1990s two rival teams of astronomers raced to find distant supernovae, one led by Saul Perlmutter and the other by Brian Schmidt, with Adam Riess as a leading member. They used the biggest telescopes in the world, together with the Hubble Space Telescope, and each expected to measure how much the expansion was slowing down. Anya liked the fact that both teams were trying to beat each other to the same answer.

In 1998 both teams discovered, to their astonishment, that the distant supernovae were fainter than they ought to have been. If the expansion had been slowing down, the explosions would have been closer and therefore brighter, but they were farther away, as though the stretching of space had been speeding up. Each team checked its results again and again for dust, for errors and for mistakes in the sums, and neither could make the surprise go away.

The only sensible conclusion was that the expansion of the universe is not slowing down but speeding up, as if a ball thrown into the air had started rising faster and faster of its own accord. Nothing in the old picture could explain it, and the discovery was so surprising that the leaders of the two teams were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011. Anya wrote the word accelerating in her notebook and drew a small rocket beside it.

Scientists gave the cause a name, dark energy, though it is really a label for our ignorance rather than an explanation. Ravi drew a pie chart with three slices: about seven tenths dark energy, about a quarter dark matter, and only a small sliver, about five percent, for all the ordinary matter. Anya looked at the sliver and said that everything she had ever seen or touched, every star and planet and person, was in that tiny piece.

Ravi drew the Greek letter lambda on the board and circled it twice, because it stands for a term that Einstein added to his equations in 1917. He called it the cosmological constant, meant to keep the universe still, and after Hubble's discovery he is said to have called it the biggest blunder of his life. Today, ironically, a constant of this kind is the simplest candidate for dark energy, so the blunder may turn out to have been a brilliant guess.

If dark energy is simply the energy of empty space, said Ravi, then quantum physics ought to tell us how much of it there is. Unfortunately the answer is larger than the measured value by a factor with more than fifty zeros, and in some versions of the sum more than a hundred. It has been called the worst prediction in the history of physics, and Ravi looked at Anya as though she might be the person to find the big idea that is waiting to be discovered.

Matter gets thinner as space stretches, said Ravi, just as the raisins in the dough drift farther apart, but dark energy seems not to thin out at all. Every new bit of space seems to come with its own share, so about five billion years ago, as the matter spread out, the push of dark energy finally became stronger than the pull of gravity. Since then the expansion has been speeding up, and it will go on speeding up as long as dark energy stays as it is.

The story is not finished, said Ravi, because in recent years a survey called DESI has measured the positions of millions of galaxies and used them to trace the history of the expansion. Its results hint that dark energy may be changing, perhaps growing weaker over billions of years, rather than staying perfectly constant. The evidence is not yet strong enough to be sure, and Ravi said that in his experience the most exciting hints are the ones that turn out to need another ten years of careful checking.

At four o'clock, with the sun now lower over the roofs, Ravi asked Anya what would happen if gravity were so strong that nothing could escape from it. To leave the Earth, he said, a rocket must reach about eleven kilometres a second, and on a heavier and denser world the speed needed would be greater still. In 1783 an English clergyman and scientist named John Michell worked out that on a star heavy enough, the escape speed would be faster than light itself, and he called such a thing a dark star.

Only weeks after Einstein published his theory, a German astronomer named Karl Schwarzschild, who was serving as a soldier on the front line of the First World War, found time to solve its equations for a round mass. His answer showed that if any mass were squeezed into a small enough ball, its gravity would trap everything, even light, and the idea was so strange that Einstein himself doubted it could be real. Schwarzschild died of an illness in 1916, never knowing how famous his solution would become.

Ravi drew a river flowing towards a waterfall, with a little boat paddling hard against the current, and he drew a chalk line across the water just before the edge. Beyond that line, he said, even the fastest paddler could not get back, and a black hole has a line like that, called the event horizon, beyond which nothing can return. At the very centre, our equations say that matter is crushed to a single point, but nobody believes that literally, and it shows only that the theories have reached their limit.

A black hole is what remains when the core of a very heavy star collapses completely, but in principle anything could become one if it were squeezed small enough. The Sun would have to be crushed into a ball about six kilometres across, and the whole Earth would have to shrink to the size of a marble, said Ravi, and he held up a real marble to show her. The Sun, he added, is far too light ever to do this by itself, so Anya need not worry about it.

People often describe black holes as vacuum cleaners that suck up everything nearby, said Ravi, but that picture is quite wrong. If the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass, the Earth would continue in its orbit just as before, because the gravity at that distance would be the same. The days would be very dark and cold, of course, and a black hole is dangerous only if you go very close, which, said Ravi, is the best argument for staying away.

Anya asked what would happen to an astronaut who fell into a black hole, and Ravi, grinning, said that the answer had a funny name. Near a small black hole, gravity pulls so much harder on your feet than on your head that you would be stretched like a strand of spaghetti, which physicists call, quite seriously, spaghettification. To a friend watching from far away, the astronaut would seem to slow down and freeze at the edge, growing dimmer and redder until the picture faded away.

Nobody can see a black hole itself, Ravi said, but the gas that is falling towards one is squeezed and heated until it glows fiercely in X-rays. In the early 1970s astronomers found that a powerful source of X-rays, called Cygnus X-1, was circling a bright blue star, and its invisible partner was too heavy to be anything but a black hole. It became the first strong candidate, though not everyone was convinced, and the physicist Stephen Hawking famously bet that it was not one, and lost.

At the very centre of our galaxy, Ravi said, a handful of stars whirl round an invisible point at astonishing speeds, and one of them, called S2, completes an orbit in just sixteen years. Two teams, led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez, tracked these stars for decades with great telescopes, and their paths showed that the hidden object has about four million times the mass of the Sun. They shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020, and the object is now called Sagittarius A star.

In 2019 the world saw the first picture of a black hole, taken by the Event Horizon Telescope, which links radio dishes all over the Earth so that together they act like a single telescope as wide as the planet. It showed a dark circle surrounded by a glowing ring of hot gas, in a galaxy called M87 about 55 million light-years away, where the black hole has the mass of some six billion Suns. In 2022 the same team published a picture of the one at the heart of our own galaxy, and Anya looked it up on her phone and held it beside the first.

Almost every large galaxy, Ravi told her, seems to have a supermassive black hole at its heart, and the more astronomers learn, the more it seems that galaxy and black hole grow up together. Some of these giants, glowing as brilliant quasars because of the gas that falls into them, already existed when the universe was less than a billion years old. That is hardly enough time, by our present understanding, for them to have grown so large, and Anya added the puzzle to her list of mysteries, which was becoming impressively long.

Ravi shook the edge of the old mattress, and a ripple ran across its surface and made the marbles tremble. Something similar happens in space, he said, for in 1916 Einstein worked out that heavy objects moving through it, such as two stars circling each other, should send out ripples called gravitational waves. He doubted that anyone would ever detect them, however, because by the time they reached the Earth the ripples would be unimaginably faint.

The first hint came in 1974, when Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a pair of neutron stars circling close round each other, one of them a pulsar that kept very accurate time. Over the years they saw that the orbit was shrinking by exactly the amount that Einstein's theory predicted if the pair were losing energy by making gravitational waves. It was strong indirect evidence, and it earned them the Nobel Prize in 1993, but nobody had yet felt a wave itself.

To catch such a faint ripple, scientists built two enormous detectors called LIGO, one in Louisiana and one in Washington State, each with two vacuum tubes four kilometres long arranged in the shape of an L. A passing wave stretches one arm very slightly and squeezes the other, and laser beams bouncing between mirrors can measure the difference, which is smaller than a thousandth of the width of a proton. Anya observed that it was like measuring the distance to the nearest star to within the width of a human hair.

On 14 September 2015, while the detectors were still being tested, both of them felt a signal that lasted barely a fifth of a second and rose in pitch like the chirp of a bird. It had been sent out by two black holes, each about thirty times as heavy as the Sun, that had spiralled together and merged more than a billion years earlier. The ripples had been travelling across space ever since, and had finally washed past the Earth early one morning.

The crash had been unimaginably violent, said Ravi, because in less than a second the mass of about three Suns was turned into gravitational waves. For that brief moment the power being released was greater than the combined light of all the stars in the observable universe, and yet it reached the Earth as a movement far smaller than the width of a proton. That, Ravi said, is how thoroughly space can muffle even the loudest events, and it is why it took a hundred years to catch one.

The scientists spent months checking and rechecking the signal before they announced it to the world in February 2016, determined not to make a mistake. In 2017 the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne, who had led the project. Since then detectors around the world have heard well over a hundred more mergers, and astronomy, said Ravi, had been looking at the universe for thousands of years and had just discovered that it could listen.

On 17 August 2017 the detectors felt a long, rising chirp, much longer than the one from the black holes, and they knew at once that it came from two neutron stars spiralling together about 130 million light-years away. Less than two seconds later, space telescopes saw a flash of gamma rays from the same part of the sky, and within hours telescopes all over the Earth were pointing in that direction. It was the first time that anyone had caught the same event both in gravitational waves and in light.

In the weeks that followed, hundreds of astronomers and dozens of telescopes, both on the ground and in space, studied the glow of the crash, which is called a kilonova. It began bright and blue and then faded to a dull red over about two weeks, just as a cloud of hot debris would do while it spread out and cooled. Anya said that she liked the idea of so many strangers, in so many countries, all looking at the same faint spot.

The colours in the fading light carried a fingerprint of heavy elements, said Ravi, and the pattern showed that the crash had made large amounts of gold, platinum and other metals that ordinary stars cannot easily produce. Collisions of neutron stars, therefore, are probably one of the main sources of such elements in the universe, though astronomers still argue about whether other violent events also contribute. The gold in a wedding ring, he told her, was probably made in such a crash, billions of years ago.

Until 2015, said Ravi, every picture of the universe had been made from light of some kind, and now there was a completely new sense, as if someone who had spent a lifetime only looking had suddenly learned to listen. Gravitational waves can come from places that light cannot escape from, such as the merger of two black holes, and they carry information that no telescope could ever collect. A space detector called LISA, which is planned for the 2030s, will listen for slower and deeper ripples than any we have heard so far.

One of the strangest results of Einstein's theory, said Ravi, is that time itself runs more slowly where gravity is stronger, so a clock in a valley ticks a little more slowly than a clock on a mountain top. In 1971 two scientists put very exact atomic clocks on passenger airliners and flew them round the world, and when they compared them with clocks that had stayed on the ground, the differences matched Einstein's predictions. Anya looked at her watch with new suspicion, and Ravi laughed and told her that it was perfectly all right for now.

The very best atomic clocks today are so precise that they can detect time running faster when they are lifted by only a few centimetres. In theory, you age very slightly faster at the top of a ladder than at the bottom. Astronauts on the space station, travelling at about eight kilometres a second, age a few thousandths of a second less in six months, and these differences are far too small to feel.

We can see only a part of the universe, said Ravi, because light from farther away has not had time to reach us in the nearly fourteen billion years since the beginning. The region that we can observe is a ball with the Earth at its centre, and because space has stretched while the light was travelling, its edge is now about 46 billion light-years away in every direction. That makes the observable universe about 93 billion light-years across, which seemed to Anya a very odd number for something that was not even supposed to be old enough.

The edge of the observable universe is not a wall or a coastline, Ravi stressed, but simply the limit of what light has had time to show us, like the horizon at sea. An observer in a galaxy far away would have a horizon of their own, centred on them, and almost certainly there is more universe beyond ours, though by its very nature we cannot see it. Anya said that this was oddly comforting, because it meant that she was not at the centre of anything.

In 1990 the Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit, high above the air that blurs the view from the ground, and the first pictures were a bitter disappointment. Its mirror had been polished to slightly the wrong shape, an error about a fiftieth of the width of a human hair, but that was enough to blur every image. In 1993 astronauts flew to the telescope in a space shuttle and fitted it with corrective optics, like a pair of spectacles, and Hubble has been sending back sharp pictures ever since.

In 1995 a group of astronomers took a risk and pointed the Hubble telescope at a patch of sky that looked completely empty, and they left it there for ten days. The patch was no bigger than a grain of sand held at arm's length, yet the picture showed about three thousand galaxies of every shape and colour, some of them among the farthest ever seen. Anya looked at the printout that Ravi had pinned to the shed door and counted until she lost her place.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on Christmas Day in 2021, has a mirror more than six metres wide, made of eighteen hexagonal segments coated in gold, which unfolded in space like a piece of origami. It floats about one and a half million kilometres from the Earth, behind a sunshield as big as a tennis court that keeps the Sun, the Earth and the Moon out of its eyes. Ravi had followed the launch live, and he admitted that he had held his breath through most of the unfolding.

Webb looks mainly at infrared light, which can slip through clouds of dust that block ordinary light, and which also carries the stretched light of the very first galaxies. To detect such faint warmth, the telescope itself has to be colder than minus two hundred degrees, or its own heat would drown out the signal, and that is the job of the sunshield. Anya remarked that it was the only telescope in history that spent its whole life trying not to be warm.

More giants are on the way, Ravi told her, among them the Extremely Large Telescope, which is being built on a mountain in the Chilean desert and will have a mirror 39 metres wide, made of hundreds of segments. In Australia and South Africa, meanwhile, thousands of radio dishes and antennas are being put up to form the Square Kilometre Array, which will map the hydrogen gas of the early universe. Every new instrument, he said, finds things that nobody had thought to ask about.

The map of our own galaxy is also being drawn in unprecedented detail, said Ravi, by a European satellite called Gaia, which has measured the positions and movements of nearly two billion stars. It uses the old method of parallax, the same trick as Anya's thumb, for millions of stars, and from their motions astronomers can now work out where whole streams of stars came from. Anya liked the thought that a trick as simple as winking at her thumb had grown into a map of a galaxy.

At a quarter to five, Ravi turned the board to the question that most people care about, which is whether other suns have worlds like ours. Until 1995 nobody had found a planet around an ordinary star, and then two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, found one that circles a star called 51 Pegasi every four days. The planet was a giant like Jupiter yet much closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun, which nobody had thought possible, and the discovery earned them the Nobel Prize in 2019.

The method, said Ravi, is the Doppler effect again, put to a new use. A planet tugs on its star as it orbits, making the star wobble slightly towards us and then away from us. The lines in the star's rainbow shift a little to red and then a little to blue, and Anya, remembering the ambulance, decided that the afternoon had a very tidy structure.

A second method, said Ravi, is simply to watch for a star to dim very slightly as a planet passes in front of it, like a moth crossing a car's headlight. The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, stared at about 150,000 stars in one patch of sky for years and found thousands of planets that way. Anya held her thumb in front of his torch and told him that she was now a planet hunter too.

More than five thousand planets around other stars have now been confirmed, said Ravi, and they are far stranger than anyone imagined, from giants hotter than a furnace to worlds of molten rock and planets that circle two suns. Astronomers now think that most stars have planets, and that our galaxy alone probably contains billions of Earth-sized worlds. Anya looked up at the pale blue sky and tried to imagine each of the invisible stars up there with its own family.

For a planet to have liquid water on its surface, said Ravi, it must be neither too close to its star nor too far away, in what astronomers call the habitable zone. A small red star called TRAPPIST-1, only about 40 light-years away, has seven planets about the size of the Earth, and three of them lie in that zone. Webb is already studying them, but it is far too early to say whether any of them has air, let alone life.

We do not even have to leave our own solar system, said Ravi, to find places where life might be possible. Moons such as Europa, which circles Jupiter, and Enceladus, which circles Saturn, hide oceans of liquid water beneath their icy crusts, and Enceladus even sprays plumes of that water into space. A passing spacecraft sampled those plumes, and a probe called Europa Clipper is on its way to study Europa, so Anya wrote the names down as the most interesting addresses in the solar system.

When a planet passes in front of its star, said Ravi, a little of the starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere. The gases in the air leave their fingerprints as dark lines in the spectrum, just as the elements in the Sun do, and Webb has already found water vapour and carbon dioxide on some distant worlds. Astronomers hope one day to find oxygen and methane together, which might be a sign of life, and there have been some excited claims, but so far none has survived careful checking.

The ingredients of life, Ravi told her, are common out in space, and in 1969 a meteorite fell near the town of Murchison in Australia carrying more than seventy kinds of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. Astronomers have since found many other carbon-rich molecules in clouds of gas between the stars, and samples brought back from asteroids have shown the same sort of material. The story of life, he suggested, might begin with a chemistry that the universe does almost everywhere.

Ingredients are not the same as a finished cake, Ravi warned, and so far we know of only one world with life on it. Life seems to have appeared on the Earth early, within a billion years or so of the planet's birth, which suggests that it may not be very hard to start. But nobody knows how it happened, and with only a single example we cannot work out how likely it is, and Anya said that she felt sorry for the scientists, who had a sample of exactly one.

In 1960 an astronomer named Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope at two nearby stars and listened for messages, and scientists have been listening on and off ever since. They have heard nothing that could be confirmed, and the strangest signal of all, a strong burst picked up in 1977 and nicknamed the Wow signal, has never been heard again. If the universe is so full of planets, people have long asked, where is everybody, and Ravi said that he found the silence more interesting than any answer.

At five o'clock the shadow of the plum tree had grown very long, and Ravi turned to a problem that bothers everyone who looks at the stars, which is how far away they are. The spacecraft Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant object that humans have ever made, more than twenty light-hours from the Earth, and it is still travelling. At its present speed it would need about 70,000 years to cover the distance to the nearest star, which Ravi said made it a very patient messenger.

The fastest object that people have ever built, said Ravi, is the Parker Solar Probe, which reaches about 190 kilometres a second as it dives close to the Sun. That sounds impressive until you do the sum, because at that speed a journey to the nearest star would still take more than six thousand years, a time longer than the whole of written history. Anya did the sum twice to be sure, and said that if she ever went, she would need a very long book.

A few engineers have a bolder idea, said Ravi, which is to send not a rocket but a swarm of probes weighing about as much as a paperclip. Each would be attached to a thin sail and pushed by a battery of powerful lasers to a fifth of the speed of light, which would take it to the nearest star in about twenty years. But the lasers, the sails and the tiny electronics that would survive the journey do not exist yet, so it is an idea, he said, and not a plan.

Anya asked about warp drives, and Ravi admitted that there is one idea that does not break the rules, at least on paper. In 1994 a physicist named Miguel Alcubierre showed that Einstein's equations allow a bubble of space that squeezes space in front of a ship and stretches it behind, carrying the ship along without anything moving faster than light inside the bubble. The catch is that it would need a kind of negative energy that nobody knows how to make, and many physicists suspect that it is simply impossible.

Anya asked whether the universe might be curved like the surface of a ball. In principle it could be curved like a ball or a saddle, said Ravi, but on the largest scales it looks almost perfectly flat. The test is to draw a giant triangle across the afterglow, using the size of its ripples as a ruler, and to measure its angles, which add up to a straight line, to within a fraction of one percent.

Flat does not necessarily mean infinite, Ravi said carefully, because a flat universe might go on for ever, or it might be finite and wrap round on itself. In the second case it would be like the screen of a video game, where a character who leaves on the right comes back on the left. We cannot tell which is true, because we see only a part of the whole, and the Earth also looks flat from a garden even though it is a ball.

What is the universe expanding into, Anya wanted to know, and what is outside it? Ravi explained that the question comes from picturing the universe as a balloon in a room, but the balloon was only a model, and the real expansion simply means that the distances between faraway galaxies are growing. Nothing outside is needed for that to happen, said Ravi, and whether there is anything outside at all is a question that nobody can answer yet.

Ravi blew a stream of soap bubbles into the air and said that some physicists think the universe may be like one of them. If inflation never stops everywhere at once, they argue, then new bubbles of space keep forming, each one a universe of its own, possibly with different rules. Nobody has found a way to test the idea, however, and a number of scientists say that until someone does, it is closer to philosophy than to science.

The numbers that describe our universe, said Ravi, seem surprisingly well suited to making stars, atoms and eventually people, since a small change in the strength of some of the forces might have left the universe without them. Some scientists take this as a hint that there are many universes and that we live in one of the few that allow observers. Others think that a deeper theory will one day explain why the numbers must be as they are, and Ravi called it a question on the border between physics and philosophy.

In 1990, as Voyager 1 was leaving the planets behind, its cameras were turned back for one last look, and they took a picture of the Earth from about six billion kilometres away. In the photograph our whole world is a pale dot, less than a single point of the picture across, caught in a beam of scattered sunlight. Anya held her notebook closed against her chest for a while, and Ravi did not say a word, because he thought that nothing he could add would improve it.

At a quarter past five, Ravi wiped the board clean with his sleeve and drew a huge clock face, because he wanted to show Anya the whole story at once. On his clock one o'clock was the Big Bang and six o'clock was the present moment, which squeezed nearly fourteen billion years into five hours, so that every minute stood for about 46 million years. He warned her that the clock was not the real time in the garden, and Anya said that she was glad, because the real time was getting short.

On the chalk clock, said Ravi, the first stars switch on a few minutes after one o'clock, and the first galaxies, including the earliest parts of the Milky Way, are gathering soon afterwards. Then the clock ticks on for hour after hour, with stars being born and dying in countless galaxies, and the Sun and the Earth are nowhere to be seen. It is a reminder, he said, that our own planet is a latecomer to the cosmic party.

It is not until twenty past four, said Ravi, that a cloud of gas and dust, enriched with the ashes of earlier stars, begins to collapse into a spinning disc. At its centre the Sun switches on, and in the disc around it, rocky grains clump together into larger and larger lumps until they become the planets, including the Earth, about four and a half billion years ago. The universe, in other words, had already been running for two thirds of its history before our planet existed.

Soon afterwards, according to the leading theory, the young Earth was struck by another planet about the size of Mars, which some scientists call Theia. The collision threw a huge cloud of molten rock into orbit, and over a short time, as these things go, the debris gathered into the Moon, which may also have helped to tilt the Earth and give it seasons. Anya looked up and, sure enough, a pale half Moon was already hanging in the blue afternoon sky.

Life appears on the clock at about twenty-three minutes to five, said Ravi, and for a very long time it consists of nothing but microscopic single cells. The oldest clear fossils, layered mats of bacteria preserved in ancient rocks in Australia, are about three and a half billion years old, and there are hints in some rocks of life that is even older. Anya looked at her own fingers and reflected that every cell in them was a distant descendant of those tiny pioneers.

Around ten past five on the clock, bacteria that used sunlight to make food began to release oxygen, and over a very long time it filled the air, in an event called the Great Oxidation. Oxygen was poison to much of the life that existed then, said Ravi, but it also made new kinds of life possible, including the larger and more complex cells with a nucleus that appeared a few minutes later. Anya took a deep breath, slowly and deliberately, as if she were thanking those ancient bacteria for every lungful.

It is almost a quarter to six, said Ravi, before the first animals appear in the sea, soft-bodied creatures that soon give way to a spectacular variety of shells, claws and eyes. By ten to six, plants have crept onto the land, followed by insects and by the first four-legged animals, and the continents begin to turn green. Anya noticed that the minutes on the clock were now much busier than the hours at the start.

The dinosaurs appear at about five minutes to six, said Ravi, and for more than three minutes they rule the land, the sea and the sky. Then, about a minute and a half before six, an asteroid some ten kilometres wide strikes the Earth near what is now Mexico, and the dust and fires and darkness that follow end the reign of nearly all of them. A few of their descendants survive to this day, he said, and Anya, who had seen a pigeon on the fence all afternoon, looked at it with real respect.

Our own species does not appear until about half a second before six o'clock, said Ravi, which is so little time that the chalk dot he made at the end of the line covered all of it. All of recorded history, from the first writing to the phone in Anya's pocket, fits into less than a hundredth of a second, and her own lifetime is far too short to draw at all. Anya, who had been feeling rather grown-up that afternoon, found that she felt both very small and oddly proud.

Ravi made a tiny cross at six o'clock, wrote the words “you are here” beside it, and stepped back to admire his work. The universe, he said, is still very young, because stars will go on being born for trillions of years, and in that time the hands of the clock would go round far more times than anyone could count. Anya asked whether they could follow the clock beyond six, and Ravi, who had been hoping she would ask, picked up the chalk again.

At half past five Ravi explained that the Sun is very slowly growing brighter, by about one part in ten every billion years, which is hardly noticeable in a lifetime. In roughly a billion years, however, it will probably be hot enough to boil away the oceans of the Earth, and long before that, plants and animals will probably be struggling. All of this, he added, lies so far in the future that humans, if they are still around, will have had plenty of time to think of something.

In about five billion years, the Sun will begin to run short of hydrogen in its core, and it will swell into a red giant more than a hundred times wider than it is now. Mercury and Venus will almost certainly be swallowed, said Ravi, and whether the Earth is swallowed or only scorched into a cinder is something that astronomers are still arguing about. Either way, he said, the garden would not be a nice place to have tea.

Then, like the stars in the glowing shells that Ravi had described earlier, the Sun will puff its outer layers into space, and its remains will shrink into a white dwarf about the size of the Earth. For a very long time that ember will go on glowing, but it will slowly cool and grow dim, and over trillions of years it will approach the temperature of its surroundings. A great deal of the Sun's story, he said, will therefore be spent in a quiet and cooling afterlife.

Andromeda is one of the few galaxies that is not moving away from us, said Ravi, because gravity is pulling it towards the Milky Way at about a hundred kilometres a second. Astronomers have long expected the two galaxies to collide in four or five billion years and to merge into one giant galaxy. Recent measurements suggest that the timing is less certain, and very few stars would hit one another in any case, so the Sun and the Earth are likely to be only spectators, if they are there at all.

Because dark energy is speeding up the expansion, said Ravi, the galaxies beyond our own neighbourhood are being carried away faster and faster, until in time their light will never reach us at all. In perhaps a hundred billion years, astronomers on a planet near a star in the merged galaxy would see nothing else in the sky, and they would find it very hard to discover that the universe had ever expanded. The universe, he said, hides its own history, and the people who live at a time when the evidence is still visible are very lucky.

Stars will go on being born for a very long time, said Ravi, but each generation uses up some of the gas, and the gas that is left is spread ever more thinly by the expansion. In about a hundred trillion years, which is thousands of times the present age of the universe, the last of the tiny red dwarf stars will burn out, and the lamps of the universe will go dark one by one. Anya wrote the number in her notebook, counted the zeros twice, and then put her pencil down for a moment.

If dark energy stays as it is now, the expansion will go on for ever, and the universe will grow ever colder, emptier and darker, an ending that physicists sometimes call the Big Freeze or the heat death. Ravi stressed that this is the most likely future according to our present knowledge, and nothing more than that. Since we do not understand dark energy, he said, the real future could still turn out to be something that nobody has imagined.

There are other possible endings, said Ravi, and he drew them as arrows on the board. In a Big Crunch the expansion would reverse and the universe would fall back together, while in a Big Rip dark energy would grow stronger and stronger until it tore apart galaxies, stars and finally atoms. The present evidence does not favour either of them, he said, but a good scientist never says never, and Anya wrote that on the board in her best handwriting.

Even black holes, said Ravi, may not last for ever, because in 1974 the physicist Stephen Hawking calculated that they should slowly leak a faint glow of particles and so lose energy and shrink. For the largest ones the process would take a number of years with about a hundred zeros, which is a stretch of time that makes the age of the universe look like the blink of an eye. Nobody has ever observed this effect, however, so it remains a prediction, but a very well respected one.

None of these endings need worry anyone alive today, said Ravi, because they lie so far beyond human history that even the whole story of our species would make hardly a scratch on the time involved. What matters more, he said, is that we happen to live in a rare and lucky moment, when the universe is old enough to have made atoms and planets and young enough to be still full of stars. Anya looked at the lawn, at the plum tree and at the old cat, and said that she would try to make the most of it.

At a quarter to six, Ravi wiped the board clean and wrote two words at the top of it, Known and Unknown, with a thick chalk line between them. Under the first he listed what has been checked a thousand times over: that the universe began almost fourteen billion years ago, that it is expanding, that stars forge the elements, and that gravity bends light and shakes space itself. It was, Anya thought, an astonishing list for a species that had only recently learned to read.

Under the second word the list grew longer and longer: what dark matter is, what dark energy is, what happened at the very first instant, why matter beat antimatter, and whether there is life anywhere else. Anya added three questions of her own, and by the time they had finished, the second column was far longer than the first and had spilled over the edge of the board. We know a great deal, said Ravi, but the honest boundary of our knowledge is long, and the best part of science is walking along it.

Anya asked how scientists can be so sure of anything, and Ravi said that they are not sure in the way that people are sure of their favourite football team. A good idea, he explained, must predict something that could turn out to be wrong, and then somebody must go and look, as astronomers looked at the eclipse of 1919 and Penzias and Wilson listened to their antenna. Ideas that survive tests of that kind earn their place, and those that do not are thrown out, however much their authors loved them.

Sometimes two excellent methods give different answers, and Ravi saved the most famous example for last. If you measure the speed of the expansion using supernovae and pulsing stars in the nearby universe, you get a figure about nine percent higher than the one that the early afterglow predicts. This gap, called the Hubble tension, has refused to close despite years of work, and it may be a hidden error or a clue to new physics, which Ravi said was the kind of puzzle that scientists dream about.

Every great advance in the afternoon's story, Ravi pointed out, began with something that did not fit. The odd orbit of Mercury led to Einstein's theory, the annoying hiss in an antenna led to the afterglow of the Big Bang, and the fast-moving stars at the edge of galaxies led to dark matter. The puzzles on the Unknown side of the board, therefore, were not failures but the places where the next discoveries were waiting.

Anya said that it seemed strange that tiny creatures on a small planet, with only a short time to live, could work out how stars burn. She added that they could even discover how the universe began, using nothing but patience, mathematics and telescopes. Ravi replied that this was the most amazing fact of the whole afternoon, and that the universe, in us, had found a way to understand itself.

Before the light faded, Ravi walked Anya to the shed door and showed her the names that he had pinned beside the posters: Leavitt, Payne, Rubin and Bell. These were the women whose measurements had changed the picture of the universe, he said, though their work had not always been welcomed at first. Behind them stood thousands of engineers, technicians and students whose names are on no poster, and every fact on the board that afternoon, he added, had been paid for with somebody's patience.

As the afternoon ended, the sky behind the roof turned from gold to pink, and the first bright point of light appeared above the chimney. Ravi said with a smile that it was really the planet Venus, though the real stars would soon follow, each one carrying light that had left it long before either of them was born. Anya sat quite still, watching the sky darken, and for once she did not feel the need to ask anything at all.

As the sky darkened, Anya asked the question that had been waiting all afternoon, which was what came before the Big Bang. Ravi smiled and admitted that nobody knows, and that scientists have several ideas but no proof. It might not even be a meaningful question, he said, but he thought that it was a fine place to end the day.

When the church clock struck six, the tea was long cold, but Anya was still at the chalkboard, filling it with questions of her own. Ravi watched her with quiet pride, knowing that the universe is still mostly unexplored. The next person to explain a piece of it might well be standing there with the chalk.
